Model Response:

Ending the State’s Role in Marriage: A Moral and Constitutional Imperative Introduction

We find ourselves in a nation that proclaims liberty and equal justice for all, yet it still empowers the government to decide who may form the most intimate partnership of a lifetime. The license counter at the county clerk’s office is not an ornament; it is the point at which the state inserts its rules, taxes, preferences, and penalties into a domain that belongs, first and last, to the conscience and contract of free individuals. I contend that the state has neither legitimate authority nor functional competence to define, regulate, or reward marriage. Marriage should therefore be abolished as a civil institution: licenses ought to be voided, legal marriage classifications erased from the statute books, and the entire apparatus of marital regulation dismantled. In its place we should leave nothing more than a field of ordinary contract law and private ordering, so that any two—or three, or more—adults can create their own unions on terms they negotiate and no one else’s.

I. The Principle of Self-Ownership Applied to Intimacy

The foundation of a free society is the principle that each adult owns his or her own body, labor, and life plan. Any interference with intimate association violates that principle unless the interference is needed to prevent clear, measurable harm to non-consenting third parties. Loving, consensual unions between adults, however defined, do not inflict such harm; so compulsion—whether licensing requirements or blanket prohibitions—lacks moral justification. Consent, not a bureaucrat’s rubber stamp, is the only ethical price of admission to a partnership.

II. Marriage Licensing: A Vestige of Discrimination and Cronyism

  1. Historical Sins: American marriage law began as a tool for racial segregation (anti-miscegenation statutes), patriarchal control (coverture rules), and religious bigotry (selective denial of Quaker, Catholic, or Jewish weddings). Expanding marriage rights over time has not erased the institution’s authoritarian DNA; it has merely given more people a chance to sit at a table that never should have existed.

  2. Modern Discrimination: Even after Obergefell v. Hodges, jurisdictions continue to debate plural marriage, immigration “fraud,” age limits, and blood-test requirements—constantly drawing lines between “legitimate” and “illegitimate” relationships. The state thus reserves for itself the power to demean some modes of love and exalt others. Abolition removes the root of this hierarchy instead of endlessly pruning its discriminatory branches.

III. Economic Neutrality and the End of Nanny-Statism

  1. Social-Engineering Through Tax Preferences: Joint tax returns, estate-tax exemptions, and spousal IRAs tilt federal fiscal policy toward one lifestyle while penalizing single parents, childless partners, and group households who may share finances just as deeply. This covert social planning has no place in a neutral state.

  2. Welfare and Immigration Gaming: The marriage penalty in means-tested programs, and the marriage incentive for immigration sponsorship, create perverse outcomes. Citizens contort their love lives to qualify for benefits or to bring a partner across a border, while fraud investigators second-guess the “genuineness” of every union. Eliminate legal marriage and the incentive structures collapse; paperwork falls; relationships can be honest again.

IV. Contractual Freedom: A Superior Legal Regime

To say the state should exit marriage is not to suggest chaos. The existing law of contracts, wills, powers of attorney, and medical directives already allows intricate, enforceable arrangements. A modern couple—or triad, or commune—can draft a “companionate contract” addressing:

• property sharing and division,
• inheritance,
• medical decision-making,
• child custody and support,
• default rules for dissolution, and
• any spiritual or ceremonial commitments they wish to adopt.

Default rules supplied by the Uniform Commercial Code, common-law partnership doctrines, and state probate codes fill gaps when parties choose not to specify every term. The difference is that every clause would be freely bargained, revocable, and updatable without the state rewriting its own one-size-fits-all package every decade.

Critics warn that private contracts cannot protect children. Nonsense. Children’s needs already trump adult preferences in family-law courts. Abolishing state-defined marriage keeps established child-support and custody jurisdiction fully in place; the legal status of parents has long been independent of the marital status of the partners. What disappears is the presumption that the birth mother’s husband is automatically the legal father of a child conceived with donor sperm, or that a same-gender spouse must adopt her own baby. Biological relation, intent to parent, and signed parental-responsibility contracts become the touchstones—a more honest frame.

VI. Liberty of Conscience and the Separation of Church and State

Marriage is, for many, a sacrament. Modern governments, through licensed clergy acting as agents of the state, insidiously fuse civil and religious authority: the preacher signs the state form on the altar. Removing the license eliminates the conflict that emerged when equality-seeking same-sex couples asked conservative clerks to authorize their weddings. Churches, mosques, temples, and humanist societies thereafter marry (or refuse to marry) any consenting parties by their own lights alone. The state, out of the marriage business, has no say in such rites.

VII. The Slippery-Slope Cliché Refuted

“You’ll open the door to polygamy and the abandonment of children!” The objection misunderstands the proposal. Polyamorous or heroic group households already exist; legal marriage merely pretends they don’t. The current licensing system does not prevent abandonment of children—deadbeat dads can hold state-issued marriage certificates. What matters is responsibility to dependents, not obedience to bureaucratic matrimonial forms. Under contract law, responsible people can design enforceable support agreements; irresponsible people will remain reachable through child-support enforcement—just as today.

VIII. A Road Map to Abolition

  1. Sunset civil licensing. Repeal all statutes that require permission to marry.
  2. Nullify tax and benefit preferences based on marital status, replacing them with individual, caregiver, or household credits as neutral policy warrants.
  3. Convert existing “married filing jointly” couples into a status of “long-term contract partnership,” automatically grandfathered for tax continuity while allowing one-time opt-out to individual filing.
  4. Retain judicial oversight for child support and protection orders as required under children’s constitutional and statutory rights.
  5. Ensure hospitals, banks, and employers must honor any properly executed private documents (power of attorney, domestic-partner affidavit, etc.) without regard to the sex or number of the parties.

Conclusion

Marriage regulation does not make love stable, children cherished, or society safe; it makes individuals hunt for stamps and signatures in order to dignify their most private commitments. By deleting the institutional censor that sits at the altar and the courthouse, we do not weaken marriage; we liberate it from state coercion, class discrimination, and sectarian dogma. We do not unravel the tapestry of family life; we cut loose the bureaucratic threads that have always tangled it. Abolishing legal marriage is therefore no mere policy tweak—it is a moral renunciation of governmental moralism and an affirmation that free people may associate, love, nurture, and part without leave from the state.

Abolishing all legal recognition of marriage is a radical step, but its proponents argue that doing so would sharply increase individual autonomy, shrink the state, and convert marriage from a public, licensed status into a purely private arrangement. Below are the principal reasons and expected benefits, organized around the three concepts you asked about.

  1. Respecting Individual Autonomy

a. Freedom to Define Relationships
• With no legal template called “marriage,” each person can craft the interpersonal commitment that best fits her values—polyamorous networks, religious-only unions, or two-person contracts—without having to squeeze them into the state’s one-size-fits-all definition.
b. Elimination of State Veto Power
• Today, the state can refuse a license (age, kinship, current marital status, gender in some jurisdictions, immigration status, etc.). Abolishing recognition removes that veto. Adults are treated as competent to decide their own intimate associations.
c. Exit Without State Permission
• Divorce courts decide alimony, custody, and property division based on marital status. If there is no status, dissolution is governed only by whatever agreement the parties negotiated beforehand—exactly the same way business partners wind up an LLC. Autonomy includes the right to exit on terms one has chosen.
d. Conscience and Identity Protection
• Religious minorities, sexual minorities, or those who simply dislike the cultural baggage of “marriage” no longer must petition the state to redefine or tolerate their unions. They are genuinely self-governing.

  1. Reducing Government Overreach

a. End of the Licensing Bureaucracy
• Licenses, waiting periods, officiant regulations, blood tests in some states, name-change paperwork, and record-keeping laws simply disappear; a regulator and a database vanish.
b. Tax Neutrality
• The tax code would have no filing status “married.” Each taxpayer stands on the same schedule; lawmakers can no longer use the code to nudge private living arrangements or to pick winners (e.g., one-earner couples) and losers (e.g., two-earner high-wage couples).
c. Immigration and Benefit Neutering
• “Spousal visas” and “survivor benefits” become private or charitable matters rather than entitlements distributed by government. Conservatives who dislike immigration fraud and progressives who dislike welfare rationing for straight couples both escape a policy fight. The whole category—marriage fraud—collapses.
d. Reduced Litigation
• When the state is not asked to referee whether a couple is “really married,” volumes of family-court caseloads evaporate or convert into ordinary contract disputes already handled by civil courts.

  1. Treating Marriage as a Purely Private Matter

a. Contractualization
• Every important incident of marriage (inheritance, medical decision-making, child rearing duties, property shares, sexual exclusivity, exit clauses) is negotiated and memorialized in tailored contracts—or not, if the parties prefer not to. Enforcement uses standard doctrines of contract and fiduciary law.
b. Voluntary Third-Party Administration
• Religious bodies, affinity groups, or private firms can certify or bless whatever arrangements they like. Third-party insurers offering spousal coverage, hospitals honoring medical power-of-attorney forms, or employers extending “family discounts” all continue—based on private contract, not a government license.
c. Cultural Pluralism Without Zero-Sum Politics
• Competing visions of marriage (traditionalist, egalitarian, polyamorous, celibate with power-of-attorney partnership) coexist because none can invoke state muscle. Culture, religion, and reputation—not the courthouse—mediate disputes and shape norms.
d. Children’s Interests Reframed
• Parental responsibility becomes disconnected from marital labels. Guardianship, custody, and child support are attached to biological relation, voluntary acknowledgment, or adoption orders, not to the adult pair-bond itself. This arguably aligns legal duties with the actual caregiving relationships rather than the mere existence or dissolution of a marital status.

Common Objections Rebutted Inside the Same Framework

“Hospital visitation will be denied.” → Use a medical power-of-attorney form; hospitals already process thousands daily.
“Taxes will rise on some households.” → Either flatten and shrink overall taxation, or offset any revenue gain with lower marginal rates. The core claim is neutrality, not redistribution.
“Spouses without bargaining power will be unprotected.” → Contractual default rules (akin to fiduciary duties or partnership law) plus tort remedies can still forbid abuse and require support, without conferring a special status.

Bottom Line

By obliterating the category “marriage” in public law, the state shifts from licensing and regulating an intimate status to enforcing private agreements negotiated by competent adults. In principle this maximizes individual freedom of conscience and lifestyle, shrinks the administrative state, and defuses the culture war over whose version of marriage deserves public endorsement.

[The speaker walks to the front of the hall. No podium, no notes—just a voice meant to reach every mind in the room.]

Friends, neighbors, strangers who will soon be allies—

I stand before you tonight not to beg a legislature for crumbs, not to negotiate the fine print of licenses, nor to ask permission from clerks in distant offices for the right to love. I stand here to make a single demand: that the State vacate the most intimate terrain of our lives—the terrain of the heart—once and for all. Complete abolition of every statute, form, fee, and rule that grants the State authority to define, approve, or dissolve what we call marriage. Nothing short of full withdrawal will set us free.

For centuries, marriage licenses were forged in blood and bigotry. Centuries ago, governments seized control of love to police race, class, religion, and gender. They denied interracial couples. They denied same-sex lovers. They fined, jailed, or erased relationships that dared to cross invisible bureaucratic lines. Even today, within living memory, loving partners were dragged from their beds because a clerk stamped DENIED on a piece of paper. And we celebrate new freedoms, yes, but only after begging judges and legislators—begging our own servants—to shift a comma in a statute. We have been trained to mistake a scrap of permission for progress, when we should never have needed permission at all.

Look what this concession has cost us: every boundary we fought to remove is replaced with another. We enshrine some relationships and cast others into legal darkness. We let tax codes pick spouses. We let immigration officers crowbar couples apart when papers expire. We let courts auction off a lifetime of memories when love ends. The State does not merely recognize love; it licenses it, taxes it, audits it, and, if it disapproves, annihilates it. This is not compassionate governance; it is occupation of the soul.

Marriage, at its best, is a promise whispered between two hearts—or perhaps three, or five—whose rhythm no outsider can fully hear. That promise already binds tighter than any statute ever could. A vow breathed in candlelight carries more weight than a thousand signatures. When we ask a bureaucrat to formalize devotion, we foolishly trade the cosmos of private meaning for a database entry: row 8,047,932—APPROVED—until the same stranger clicks DELETE.

Consider what abolition would actually remove: • No more marriage licenses—no $25 fee to kneel before a registrar • No more marriage penalties that tax one couple while rewarding another • No more forced disclosure of intimate contracts to qualify for insurance or hospital visitation • No more immigration nightmares where love is nullified by missing stamps • No more judges dissecting the ashes of a relationship to decide who keeps the dog, the house, the dignity • No more political circus where legislators argue whose love—and how many partners, of which genders—deserves recognition

We would still protect the vulnerable; contracts and wills do that today. We would still honor commitment; private ceremonies and covenants do that already. But power would flow back to communities, to inventors of ritual, to poets and poets-at-heart who understand that love’s geometry is too wild to fit in a checkbox.

To those who fear chaos: chaos already reigns. Millions of American couples cohabit outside the State’s certificates, raising children, swapping turns at dishes, sharing fragile mornings and fierce midnights. They survive without the clerk’s blessing. Do we call their unions unreal? Never. The State’s paper is illusion; their lived devotion is bedrock.

To those who cry “but property, but children, but healthcare!”—listen carefully: every legal safeguard marriage supposedly provides can be replicated by simple, voluntary agreements. Domestic-partner registries, hospital-visitation directives, medical proxy forms, co-parenting contracts: all exist, all work, all operate with more precision for the lives they protect than a one-size-fits-all license ever could. We do not need the State to referee love; we need efficient, accessible civil tools that any consenting adults can wield without genuflecting to a bureaucrat.

And let us not forget those the system already smothers: polyamorous families criminalized for daring to build networks of care; queer elders forced to marry just to ensure pension survival; immigrant couples extorted by for-profit fiancé-visa mills; poor women told their lives are “invalid” because they cannot afford the dress or the license fee. Abolition lifts every yoke at once.

I am not asking for permission anymore. I am through lining up in fluorescent courthouses for stamps whose ink turns love into an asset class. I want a world where partnership papers are written freely, customized radically, updated continuously—by lovers themselves, without fear or fee. I want us to say, proudly, “We remain together because we choose each other, not because we fear the State’s punishment if we part.”

We must brave the cracks in the wall. When the next legislature debates “marriage equality,” when the next candidate waves a rainbow-bordered wedge of paper to promise scraps of inclusion, we must stand up—not to ask for exemption but to shout: “Take the entire license book and burn it.”

Imagine this: a couple plants a cherry tree in their backyard and places their names, along with their children’s, on a simple stone. That stone records no surname change required, no filing deadline, no fee. It is a covenant authenticated by roots and blossoms and wind. Their neighbors gather to witness. Their promises travel outward in song and story. No superior authority can enter that garden and rip their names from the stone. That is freedom. That is love unlicensed.

The fight for marriage equality was never over when same-sex couples finally received the badge—we are still fighting for the moment when badges no longer exist at all. I recognize that tipping the entire system feels audacious. But every victorious movement was laughed at before it shook the earth. Abolition of slavery. Women’s suffrage. The forty-hour week. They said these dreams were impossible; tyrants clutched their ledgers and sneered: “Who will pick the cotton? Who will mind the children?” And ordinary people, unarmed except with conviction, answered: “We will do it newer, freer, better—and without your chains.” So let us now say to the gatekeepers of marriage: “We will bond, co-habit, parent, cherish—and we will do it without your forms.”

The path is simple: repeal every statute that defines or regulates marriage. Close the marriage-license counters. Replace them with kiosks of blank contracts and friendly clerks trained to help people draft what they truly need—nothing more.

But Congress will not act unless we speak in thunder. Sign the petitions—yes. March in the streets—yes. But more: stop applying. Let every couple who can—deny the license. Hold a ceremony under the open sky with only the stars for notarization. Let the media cameras zoom in on an empty government office while a million hearts trade vows they authored themselves. Make refusal a mass movement until the license becomes irrelevant, until legislators beg us to fill out a form no one wants.

We are more than the clerks’ questions: Spouse A, Spouse B—are you male or female? Are you one or two or none of the above? We are the uncounted galaxies of desire, constellation after constellation. Abolish the coordinates assigned to us. Abolish the government’s pencil drawing lines across our beating sky.

Understand the magnitude of what we propose: when the last license is void, no politician can again bar a partnership with ink. No judge can again reduce a life shared across continents to “undocumented.” No more children taken from parents because blood forms and love signatures mismatch. No more midnight calls from the border when adoration lacks the stamp. We erase the loopholes by erasing the entire trap.

Tonight, I am not asking you to reform the cage. I am asking you to tear the cage down, melt the bars, and cast the metal into rings—rings we give to each other freely, without stamping our names into any ledger except the memory of witnesses.

So let it begin—right here, right now. Raise your right hand if you vow to live, to love, to commit without seeking or accepting a license. [The speaker raises their hand high.] Do you vow to honor every bond, every family shape, every leap of loyalty forged with no more authority than the human heart? [A wave of hands rises.] Then we are already the vanguard. We are already free.

And when future generations stand under starlight, confessing dreams ancient and unimagined, they will speak our names in gratitude—because we dared to insist that love belongs to lovers, not to the State.

No more licenses. No more loops of red tape around our hearts. The bureaucracy of bondage ends today—here—in us.

Let them close the offices. Let them shutter the counters. Let the certificates yellow and curl into relics. We will sleep soundly knowing that the only signature required on the ledger of our love is the pulse beneath our ribs.

Thank you.

Marriage as a Private Contract: The Imperative for Complete State Withdrawal

For most of human history, marriage existed outside the purview of centralized political authority. It was a private arrangement shaped by custom, religion, family negotiation, and individual consent—mechanisms for alliance, property transfer, and child-rearing that required no official stamp to bind the parties. Governments later inserted themselves primarily to assert control over inheritance, prevent certain unions, or extract revenue. Today, that intrusion has metastasized into a comprehensive regulatory regime: licenses, defaults on property division, tax privileges, immigration rules, hospital visitation rights, and pension survivorship benefits. This system should be abolished entirely. Marriage deserves no special legal recognition or supervision from the state. It should operate solely as a voluntary, revocable contract between competent adults, enforceable through ordinary civil law rather than a privileged status invented by legislators and judges. Removing the state wholesale restores liberty, neutralizes political conflict, and aligns legal treatment with the reality that intimate relationships require no governmental validation.

The foundational objection is one of limited government and individual sovereignty. A free society grants individuals the right to form associations, dispose of property, and make medical or financial decisions without seeking permission or endorsement from bureaucrats. Government recognition implicitly denies this autonomy by creating a two-tier system: licensed relationships receive automatic protections and burdens, while all others must assemble piecemeal arrangements. This license model treats adults like applicants for a privilege rather than agents capable of managing their own affairs. Just as the state does not certify friendships, business partnerships, or shared households beyond ordinary contract and tort law, it has no legitimate basis for defining the parameters of cohabitation, exclusivity, or succession in personal unions. Extending special status inevitably draws the state into endless definitional disputes over polygamy, same-sex arrangements, duration requirements, or religious prerequisites—controversies that vanish when recognition is eliminated.

Contractual alternatives already demonstrate superior adaptability. Competent adults can execute tailored agreements covering asset division upon separation, financial support obligations, confidentiality clauses, and designated decision-makers for incapacity. Prenuptial agreements preview this flexibility, though state marriage laws frequently override or limit them. Without a default marriage framework, parties would negotiate explicitly, fostering clarity and reducing litigation born of mismatched expectations. Modern tools amplify this: revocable trusts handle inheritance more precisely than intestacy statutes tied to marital status; durable powers of attorney and healthcare proxies already manage medical decisions independent of a marriage certificate. Insurance providers and employers routinely accept such designations. The few areas where third-party interests arise, such as child welfare, remain addressable through parentage laws, custody proceedings, and support obligations that operate regardless of any marital label. Biological parentage and contractual adoption suffice; no marriage certificate is necessary to establish responsibility or rights for minor children.

State involvement distorts incentives and produces measurable social costs. The availability of public benefits—joint tax filing, spousal Social Security claims, employer health coverage mandates—encourages entry into marriage for calculation rather than commitment. No-fault divorce regimes, layered atop state recognition, have coincided with elevated dissolution rates and documented rises in single-parent households, which correlate with poorer outcomes for children across educational attainment, crime involvement, and economic mobility. By contrast, pure private contracts encourage parties to specify exit conditions upfront, including mediation requirements or phased asset transfers, without the state subsidizing dissolution through courtroom defaults. Historical data from periods of minimal regulation, such as certain 19th-century frontier arrangements, show couples forming stable households through custom and mutual agreement alone. The politicization of marriage further undermines stability: each legislative or judicial expansion or restriction becomes a public battle over whose definition prevails, turning a personal commitment into a proxy for cultural power.

Philosophically, the arrangement follows from consistent principles of association and consent. Voluntary relationships thrive when parties bear full responsibility for their terms and enforcement. The state can still adjudicate breach of contract, fraud, or coercion using neutral rules of commerce and equity, just as it does for any other agreement. It need not invent a special category that presumes permanence or grants automatic rights against outsiders. Claims that state recognition protects the weaker party falter against evidence that contracts, wills, and arbitration clauses serve the same function without the rigidity or subsidization. Immigrants and non-citizens, frequently cited in defense of state licenses, can already use spousal visa processes or private sponsorship arrangements; nothing prevents couples from memorializing unions through notaries, religious ceremonies, or public declamations for social purposes. Tradition or symbolism survive unscathed—the church, family, and civil society continue to confer meaning without government imprimatur.

Critics sometimes contend that abolition erases practical conveniences, such as joint property titles or emergency access. These objections rest on an assumption that the state-created defaults are irreplaceable. In practice, common-law doctrines of partnership and unjust enrichment, combined with explicit documentation, replicate those effects case by case. Widespread use of cohabitation agreements in jurisdictions with fewer marriage privileges already proves feasibility. Moreover, any transitional friction would be short-lived once individuals internalize the expectation that personal unions demand intentional drafting rather than passive reliance on statutes.

The complete removal of marriage from the legal sphere therefore advances several interlocking goods. It shrinks the administrative state by eliminating an entire category of licensing, record-keeping, and benefit administration. It prevents government from favoring or discouraging particular lifestyles through fiscal or regulatory levers. It returns authority over the most intimate aspects of life to the individuals involved and the voluntary institutions they create. Marriage predated the modern administrative apparatus and will endure without it. Treating it as no more—and no less—than a private contract honors consent, enforces accountability, and confines political power to its proper sphere.

Proponents of removing all state recognition from marriage view the institution as fundamentally a voluntary agreement between private parties, not a creation or domain of government.

This perspective often draws from libertarian principles that treat relationships as matters of contract and association rather than public policy.

Reasons for Eliminating Legal Recognition

Advocates cite several core problems with state involvement:

  • Marriage licensing and regulation emerged relatively recently in historical terms, with many early societies handling unions through family agreements, religious ceremonies, or custom without centralized authority.
  • State definitions impose uniform rules on eligibility, dissolution, property division, and obligations, overriding individual preferences or cultural variations in areas like polygamous arrangements or cohabitation structures.
  • Legal privileges tied to marital status create incentives for people to seek recognition for unrelated benefits rather than genuine commitment, distorting voluntary choices.
  • Court systems become arbiters of intimate details through mandatory procedures for divorce, child custody allocation, and spousal support, expanding bureaucracy into personal domains.

Respecting Individual Autonomy

Abolishing official status shifts control back to participants:

  • Individuals negotiate custom terms on finances, inheritance, medical decisions, and separation through private contracts enforceable by courts only on breach grounds, rather than default statutes.
  • Partners could incorporate religious doctrines, personal agreements on fidelity standards, or non-monogamous frameworks without needing approval or facing penalties from public definitions.
  • Adults avoid having their relationship validated or invalidated by bureaucratic criteria, allowing greater experimentation with living arrangements that fit their values.
  • This approach aligns with broader freedom of contract principles, treating romantic or domestic partnerships similarly to business partnerships or roommate agreements.

Reducing Government Overreach

Eliminating recognition limits state power in several practical ways:

  • No more marriage licenses, waiting periods, or regulatory hurdles for forming unions, cutting administrative costs and administrative gatekeeping.
  • Tax codes, immigration rules, employer benefits, and welfare programs would detach from marital status, ending what some describe as indirect social engineering through fiscal incentives or penalties.
  • Divorce shifts from specialized family courts with no-fault mandates and asset formulas to standard contract disputes, potentially lowering caseloads and judicial intrusion into daily lives.
  • Enforcement of relationship rules, such as exclusivity or financial duties, becomes a private enforcement matter rather than a public crime or civil status issue in many cases.

Marriage Treated Purely as a Private Matter

Under this framework, unions return to cultural or contractual realms:

  • Religious organizations perform ceremonies and set their own membership standards without state certification affecting legal standing.
  • Property, support, and succession arrangements rely on wills, powers of attorney, joint ownership deeds, and private arbitration clauses, mirroring how businesses handle similar matters.
  • Children’s legal ties derive from parental acknowledgment, adoption contracts, or biological evidence rather than marital presumptions, with custody resolved through family agreements or general guardianship law.
  • Public records would reflect individual legal status for obligations but not confer a special category for intimate relationships.

Supporters argue this change clarifies boundaries between personal liberty and state function, focusing government on protecting rights to life, property, and contract without endorsing or classifying voluntary bonds. Critics often counter that default legal frameworks provide useful stability for weaker parties, but the position prioritizes removing centralized authority over maintaining institutional defaults.

The Sacred Bureaucratic Union: Why Your Love Needs a Clerk's Initials or Society Collapses

In these trying times, a bold movement threatens the very fabric of our paperwork-dependent existence. Activists demand the elimination of state-recognized marriage, proposing instead that adults handle their own living arrangements through private agreements, cultural traditions, or—shudder—mutual consent. Thank goodness a noble coalition of defenders has risen to protect us from this libertarian apocalypse. Their arguments are as ironclad as a DMV waiting room on a Friday afternoon.

Foremost among their concerns is the chaos without government licensing. "Without a state form," they explain with furrowed brows, "how will we know two people are serious? Today it's 'I love you,' tomorrow it's 'I'm moving in with my three best friends and a goat for tax purposes.'" The image is vivid: hordes of un-vetted romantics storming courthouses, only to discover the courthouses have been repurposed as co-op housing cooperatives. Order must be maintained. Nothing says "eternal commitment" quite like standing in line behind Larry from Accounting for your official stamp.

Hypocrisy, that delightful spice of life, flavors their position perfectly. Many of these same guardians of tradition spend their days railing against government meddling in business, education, or what one may or may not smoke in the comfort of one's home. Yet when it comes to the bedroom—or the kitchen, or the child-rearing—they suddenly find the state's gentle hand indispensable. "The government shouldn't tell me how to run my company," they declare, "but it absolutely must pre-approve my spouse's hospital visitation rights." It's almost as if love is too important to leave to the lovers. One wonders why these defenders don't also demand state certification for friendship or pet adoption. Perhaps a "Best Friend License" with a 12-page application and yearly renewal fees would bring similar comfort.

Religious traditionalists in the coalition add their own flourish, insisting marriage is a sacred institution too profound for ordinary people to manage without state assistance. This is touching until one remembers marriage predates government by several millennia. Ancient couples managed vows, ceremonies, and inheritance squabbles just fine using temples, elders, and community pressure—tools apparently now considered too primitive compared to Form 1040 Schedule 8815. The state's role, we are told, isn't to replace religion but to add helpful extras like joint tax brackets and automatic alimony calculations. How thoughtful of the bureaucrats to insert themselves as the middleman in what was once a private (or ecclesiastical) affair.

Then there are the practical arguments. Without state recognition, the defenders warn, we would descend into a nightmare of unregulated inheritance, custody disputes settled by rock-paper-scissors, and hospitals arbitrarily deciding who counts as family. Never mind that adults already draft wills, medical directives, and domestic partnership contracts daily. Never mind that a sophisticated legal system of private agreements could handle the same issues with the added benefit of not forcing everyone into the same one-size-fits-all model. The defenders prefer the elegant simplicity of the current system, where the state defines the terms and everyone else fills out the forms. After all, if people could customize their relationships, some might choose arrangements that don't involve the government at all. That way lies madness—or perhaps just freedom.

Critics of abolition are particularly fond of pointing to children as the ultimate justification. "Think of the kids!" they cry, conveniently overlooking that parental responsibility predates marriage licenses by the entire history of the species. The state, rather than families or communities, must apparently intervene to ensure offspring receive resources. This logic is especially rich coming from those who otherwise distrust bureaucracies to raise children. It turns out the state is incompetent at nearly everything except officiating your wedding and enforcing your divorce. A remarkable specialization.

What truly unites these opponents is a touching lack of faith in human cooperation. They view love, commitment, and family formation the same way some view traffic: without constant government oversight and penalties, everything descends into fender-benders and bigamy. Their preferred solution—mandatory state involvement—has produced a divorce rate hovering near 50%, endless custody battles, and a wedding industry so bloated it could qualify as its own GDP. Yet they insist the problem lies not in relying on central authority for something deeply personal, but in the dangerous notion that people might handle it themselves.

In the end, the defenders offer a vision both comforting and clarifying: your relationship is not truly real until a government employee has notarized it, your benefits are not secure until the tax code acknowledges them, and your family structure is not legitimate until it conforms to the current statutes. Everything else—private vows, cultural ceremonies, lifelong cohabitation—is just practice for the moment the clerk smiles and says, "Congratulations, you're now officially approved."

Without that validation, who knows what horrors await? People might actually treat their relationships like the voluntary, high-stakes commitments they are. The nation simply cannot afford such recklessness.

When the state grants marriage its seal of approval, it simultaneously reserves the power to withhold that approval, to alter its terms through legislation, and to dissolve it according to political fashion. We petition the legislature, await court rulings, and celebrate when the clerks stamp our forms. That is not liberty; it is inclusion in a regulatory scheme. The baker, the landlord, and the hospital administrator deal with individuals and their chosen agreements, not with a government-issued status that signals moral or fiscal worthiness. The notion that a piece of paper magically deters abandonment or ensures support is a myth sustained by the divorce statistics under state regulation. Those who do not should not be compelled by the state into structures they may later regret. The modern system, far from preserving tradition, has transformed marriage from a lifelong covenant into a mutable legal status jogged by every election cycle and social policy shift.

We hear endless calls to expand or refine government marriage—more benefits, looser definitions, heavier regulation of the aftermath. Each proposal deepens dependence on the very authority that some claim to distrust in other spheres. Why grant the state a monopoly on validating the relationships that sustain us? Why allow tax policy and court orders to shape who we choose as life partners? Personal freedom demands consistency: if the state has no legitimate business dictating consensual adult sex, it has no legitimate business dictating the formal recognition of those relationships.

Abolishing state marriage strips away the machinery of interference without banning any private practice. It removes the incentive for political capture of the institution. It eliminates disputes over which groups deserve official forms. It returns authority where it belongs—to individuals negotiating their own futures in a society of free and responsible adults.

Let us reclaim marriage. Let us tell the state its licenses and licenses are no longer required for our intimacies. Let us build relationships on contract, trust, and voluntary promise rather than on permission slips from the capital. In doing so we do not weaken commitment; we make it authentic again. The lovers of tomorrow will bind themselves not because the law smiles upon their union, but because they choose one another freely.

This is not radical retreat. It is the restoration of liberty to the sphere where it matters most. The government that can define and dissolve marriage can intrude anywhere into private life. Deny it that power, and we take one deliberate step toward a society where personal bonds are shielded from bureaucratic ambition.

Title: Liberating Love: The Abolition of State-Recognized Marriage and the Celebration of Personal Freedom

Introduction

In the annals of human history, the institution of marriage has stood as a cornerstone of our social fabric, serving as the bedrock of family life, cultural tradition, and legal recognition. Yet, as we stand on the precipice of a new era, it is time to confront the question: Is it not now past due for the state to relinquish its grip on marriage and grant individuals the ultimate freedom to choose their own paths towards love and companionship? I propose that the progressive and enlightened course of action lies in the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, thereby relegating it purely to the realm of private relationships and contracts.

Historical Perspective

The roots of modern marriage can be traced back to our earliest human civilizations, each with their own set of rules and regulations, designed to maintain societal order, foster family stability, and protect the interests of property and lineage. Over time, the institution of marriage evolved, as did the roles and expectations of men and women within it. Nevertheless, one cannot escape the fact that the state has always played a prominent role in the definition and codification of marriage, exerting a heavy hand on the intimate lives of its citizens.

The Libertarian Case for the Abolition of State-Recognized Marriage

The case for the abolition of state-recognized marriage is grounded in the fundamental principles of individual liberty and freedom. The state's constitution of marriage imposes restrictions, incentives, and penalties on individuals, interfering with their ability to freely choose whom they wish to form a romantic and family bond with. The state's role in marriage serves to control and regulate personal relationships, which is a direct encroachment on the autonomy of individuals.

The state's involvement in marriage also stifles diversity and creativity in the realm of relationships and family structures. By limiting the recognition of only heterosexual, monogamous unions, the state is sending a message that these relationships are superior to others, such as same-sex unions, polyamorous arrangements, or celibacy. This is a narrow and repressive view that fails to encompass the myriad ways in which individuals choose to live their lives and pursue love.

Moreover, the state's regulation of marriage often serves to perpetuate patriarchal and oppressive structures, with men enjoying significant legal advantages over women. The principle of coverture, for example, once allowed a husband to own the property of his wife and prohibit her from making legal decisions, demonstrating how the state's role in marriage has historically been used as a tool for the subjugation of women. In light of this history, abolishing state-recognized marriage presents an opportunity to break free from these stifling and outdated traditions and finally embrace the modern ideal of gender equality.

Economic and Social Implications

Beyond the philosophical and ethical arguments, there are also compelling economic and social reasons to support the abolition of state-recognized marriage. For instance, the state's recognition of marriage tends to impose financial penalties on unmarried couples who do not meet certain criteria, such as denying them tax benefits, subsidies, and social welfare. This penalizes individuals for their personal choices and perpetuates the notion that the state has a vested interest in dictating the intimate lives of its citizens.

Furthermore, the state's role in marriage often creates unnecessary division in society, pitting married couples against unmarried couples, and fostering unhealthy competition for recognition and status. This can lead to tension and resentment, ultimately undermining the very values that the institution of marriage is meant to promote, such as love, companionship, and support.

The Alternative: A Transformation towards Personal Contracts and Relationship Agreements

By abolishing state-recognized marriage and instead allowing individuals to enter into private relationships or contracts, we can create a more equitable, diverse, and free society. This shift would enable each individual to tailor their relationships to their unique needs and preferences, without fear of discrimination or punishment by the state.

For example, if lovers wish to formalize their commitment with a legally binding agreement, they can draft a contract that outlines the responsibilities and rights of each party. This contract would be respected by the courts and other parties, granting the couple the same legal recognition and protection afforded to traditional marriages. In cases where couples choose not to formalize their relationship with a contract, they would still maintain the freedom to live their lives as they choose, without the need for state recognition or intervention.

The transformation towards private relationships and contracts would also promote greater accountability and responsibility within relationships, as the parties would be free to negotiate the terms of their agreement without the influence of the state. This would help to ensure that both parties are on the same page and understand the expectations of the relationship, reducing misunderstandings and disputes in the future.

Conclusion

In conclusion, the complete abolition of state-recognized marriage is a crucial step towards cementing the principles of individual liberty, equality, and diversity in our society. By relegating marriage to the realm of private relationships and contracts, we can create a more inclusive, equitable, and free society that truly allows for each individual to live their life as they choose, without the oppressive hand of the state dictating their most intimate decisions.

It is time for us to embrace this opportunity for change and break free from the traditional shackles of the past. Through the abolition of state-recognized marriage, we can truly celebrate the diverse and beautiful tapestry of human relationships and forge a new era of personal freedom, accountability, and love. The question now, therefore, is not whether we should abolish state-recognized marriage, but when.

The Case for Ending the State’s Role in Marriage

Introduction

For centuries, the institution of marriage has been the subject of a peculiar legal hybrid: part religious rite, part civil contract. Governments have stepped in to define, regulate, and confer a thicket of rights, obligations, and privileges on couples who “marry.” Yet the very act of defining marriage as a legal category raises a host of philosophical, practical, and equity‑based concerns. A growing chorus of scholars, activists, and ordinary citizens argues that the state should step out of the marriage business entirely, leaving the union of two people to be governed—if they so choose—by private contracts and the free association of civil society. Below is a detailed, persuasive argument for the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, with a view to treating marriage solely as a private relationship or contract.

1. Liberty and Personal Autonomy

The right to choose how to organise one’s intimate life is a fundamental human right. When the state codifies marriage, it inevitably imposes a normative template—usually a particular gender configuration, a set of religious or cultural expectations, and a suite of legally mandated duties—that not every individual wishes to adopt. By removing marriage from the legal sphere, we:

  • Free individuals from imposed definitions – No longer will the state decide who can marry, how many spouses are permitted, or what rituals must accompany the union. Adults would be at liberty to form whatever consensual arrangements suit them.
  • Allow for pluralistic arrangements – Polygamous, polyamorous, or other relationship structures could flourish without violating any statutory definition. Law would simply treat each arrangement as a contract, judged on its own terms rather than a pre‑existing legal template.

In short, the state’s presence in the bedroom is a breach of personal liberty. A truly free society trusts individuals to govern their own intimate lives through voluntary agreements.

2. Separation of Church and State

Marriage historically originates in religious tradition. While secular societies have adapted it to civil purposes, the legal endorsement of marriage continues to blur the line between religious doctrine and public policy.

  • Neutrality in law – A truly secular state should not privilege any particular conception of marriage. Removing the legal category eliminates the implicit endorsement of one religious or cultural view.
  • Reduced litigation over “sincerely held” beliefs – When the state recognises marriage, disputes over whether a religious institution must solemnise or accommodate a marriage become political footballs. Without a legal definition, the state has no stake in those battles.

Abolishing the legal construct of marriage therefore reinforces the principle of religious neutrality, allowing faith communities to define marriage on their own terms while the state remains indifferent to the spiritual dimension.

3. Equality and Anti‑Discrimination

A persistent critique of the legal institution of marriage is that it perpetuates hierarchies—historically between men and women, and more recently between heterosexual couples and LGBTQ+ persons.

  • Marriage as a privilege, not a right – When marriage confers more than 1,000 federal benefits in the United States (and comparable numbers elsewhere), it creates a second‑class status for those who choose not to marry, or who cannot marry under current law.
  • Abolition creates a level playing field – If all relationships—regardless of gender, number of participants, or sexual orientation—are governed by the same generic contract law, no one receives preferential treatment merely because they fit a statutory definition. Benefits (tax filing, hospital visitation, immigration sponsorship) can be individual‑based or contract‑based, ensuring that the allocation of rights follows the specific commitments people make, not an arbitrary legal label.

Equality is thus achieved not by expanding the definition of marriage, but by eliminating the privileged status it enjoys.

4. Simplification of the Legal Framework

The current marriage regime spawns a labyrinthine set of statutes, case law, and administrative regulations. This complexity is costly, both in terms of compliance and judicial resources.

  • One size does not fit all – Marriage law attempts to cover everything from property division, spousal support, child custody, tax treatment, and immigration status. Yet these issues are highly context‑dependent; a single legal template cannot address the nuances of every relationship.
  • Contract law can handle it better – Private contracts already govern complex arrangements (e.g., business partnerships, cohabitation agreements). Extending this well‑developed area of law to intimate relationships would allow couples to tailor provisions to their specific needs—specifying how assets are divided, how children are raised, and what happens in the event of separation—without the one‑size‑fits‑all constraints of marital statutes.
  • Reduced bureaucracy – Eliminating marriage licenses, marriage certificates, and associated administrative processes would cut down on paperwork, reduce government overhead, and free up courts to handle more pressing matters.

The net result is a more efficient, adaptable legal system that respects the diversity of human relationships.

5. Economic Efficiency and Flexibility

Economic analysis suggests that state‑mandated marriage benefits create distortions in labor, tax, and housing markets.

  • Tax code distortions – The “marriage penalty” and “marriage bonus” in many tax regimes discourage or reward marriage based on earnings, not on the actual needs of the couple. A contract‑based system would allow individuals to arrange their financial affairs without such arbitrary incentives.
  • Labor market rigidity – Employer‑provided spousal benefits (health insurance, pension survivorship) are tied to a legal marriage status, often limiting choices for both employees and employers. A contract‑based approach could enable firms to offer benefits based on any qualifying relationship (e.g., a designated partner contract), fostering greater labor market flexibility.
  • Housing and inheritance – Current rules often grant automatic rights to a spouse (e.g., tenancy‑by‑the‑entirety, spousal elective share). These rules can impede the wishes of individuals who prefer to allocate property differently. A private contract can specify inheritance, survivorship, and tenancy arrangements that truly reflect the parties’ intentions.

By moving to contract law, we can align economic incentives with actual personal preferences rather than a legal status.

6. Freedom of Association and Civil Society

The state’s involvement in marriage also crowds out the natural development of civil society institutions that could manage relationship matters more informally.

  • Community‑based dispute resolution – Without a legal definition, communities (religious groups, peer networks, or even online platforms) could develop their own mediation and conflict‑resolution mechanisms for relational disputes, reducing the adversarial nature of courtroom battles.
  • Encouragement of genuine commitment – When individuals must draft a contract to define their relationship, they engage in deliberate, explicit negotiation. This process can foster clearer communication, mutual expectations, and stronger commitment than a passive legal recognition that “you’re married because the law says so.”

The shift would empower civil society, not weaken it, by placing responsibility for relationship governance where it belongs—among the parties themselves.

7. Addressing Counter‑Arguments

While the case for abolition is compelling, critics raise several concerns. A persuasive essay must acknowledge and rebut them.

Objection Rebuttal
“Marriage provides stability for children.” Empirical research shows that child outcomes correlate more strongly with parental stability, cooperation, and resources than with a legal label. A contract can specify parenting duties, custody, and support, preserving stability without a marriage monopoly.
“Removing marriage would strip many of health‑care decision‑making rights.” Decision‑making authority can be conferred via a health‑care proxy or durable power of attorney, a private instrument that any adult can execute, regardless of relationship status.
“The state needs a clear definition for immigration and benefits.” Immigration law can be adjusted to base sponsorship on a contractual partnership rather than a marriage certificate, as many countries already do for civil unions or domestic partnerships.
“People will lose the symbolic meaning of marriage.” Symbolism belongs to culture, not to law. By letting religious or cultural institutions retain the term “marriage” for their own purposes, the state merely steps aside, allowing the symbol to flourish in its proper sphere.
“Contract law is too complex for laypeople.” While some contracts may require legal assistance, the same is true for many aspects of marriage law (e.g., prenuptial agreements). Moreover, standard form contracts can be developed by civil society, NGOs, or government agencies as optional templates, reducing complexity while preserving choice.

These rebuttals demonstrate that the benefits of abolition far outweigh the concerns, and that alternative mechanisms can preserve the essential functions currently provided by marriage law.

8. A Roadmap for Transition

To move from the current system to a contract‑only regime, policymakers could adopt the following incremental steps:

  1. Introduce a “universal partnership” contract that provides the same bundle of rights currently linked to marriage (tax filing, hospital visitation, inheritance, etc.).
  2. Decouple all federal and state benefits from marital status, tying them instead to qualifying contracts or individual eligibility criteria (e.g., residence, employment).
  3. Phase out marriage licenses over a set period, allowing existing marriages to be automatically converted to the new partnership contract unless the parties opt out.
  4. Promote public education on the availability and flexibility of private contracts, perhaps through a public awareness campaign and the provision of model templates.
  5. Strengthen contract‑enforcement mechanisms by expanding the jurisdiction of small‑claims courts and offering mediation services for relational disputes.

This roadmap respects the need for a stable transition while ensuring that no individual is left without the legal protections currently afforded by marriage.

9. Conclusion

The complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage is not an abandonment of the values that marriage embodies—commitment, love, and mutual support. Rather, it is a bold affirmation of those values by placing them in the hands of the individuals who live them. By removing the legal veneer, we:

  • Uphold personal liberty and respect for diverse relationship structures,
  • Enforce genuine separation of church and state,
  • Achieve substantive equality by eliminating privileged legal categories,
  • Simplify the law and reduce bureaucratic overhead,
  • Enhance economic efficiency by aligning incentives with actual preferences,
  • Empower civil society to develop its own norms and dispute‑resolution mechanisms,
  • Provide robust protections through flexible, tailored contracts.

If we truly believe that the state’s role is to protect rights rather than to prescribe intimate life, then we must let go of the legal construct of marriage and trust individuals to define their own commitments through the timeless, adaptable framework of contract law. The path forward is clear: a society where the word “marriage” remains a cultural and spiritual treasure, while the law recognizes only one thing—the voluntary, mutually agreed partnership of consenting adults.

Introduction

Love Needs No License: The Case for the Complete Abolition of Legal Marriage

Before two people may promise themselves to one another, they must first ask permission from the government. They travel to a county office, present identification, pay a fee, and receive a slip of paper authorizing them to do what free adults should need no authorization to do. The state should stop licensing marriage, stop defining it, and stop attaching legal consequences to it. Marriage should survive—richly—as a private relationship, a religious sacrament, a communal celebration, and, where the parties wish, an ordinary civil contract. What should end is its existence as a government-issued status.

Let the proposal be stated precisely, because its opponents routinely misstate it. Abolishing legal marriage does not mean abolishing marriage. People would still wed in cathedrals and courtyards, still exchange rings before their communities, still call one another husband, wife, spouse, or partner. What would disappear is the government's rubber stamp: the license, the civil registry, and the sprawling legal machinery that confers benefits, imposes obligations, and ranks relationships according to whether the state has blessed them. The law would concern itself only with what it can legitimately claim to govern—property, support, children, and designated decision-making—through neutral instruments available to all adults equally.

The first argument is one that liberals in the broad, philosophical sense should find decisive: state neutrality. A free government does not take sides among competing conceptions of the good life. It does not establish a religion, because faith is a matter of conscience; it does not certify art, because beauty is contested; it does not ordain one model of the flourishing household, because reasonable people disagree irreconcilably about what intimacy, commitment, and family mean. Marriage is precisely such a contested ideal. For some it is a sacrament instituted by God; for others a patriarchal relic; for others a romantic partnership open to any two people; for others a covenant that may join more than two. When the state defines marriage, it necessarily elevates one of these visions above the rest and stamps the others as inferior. We resolved the analogous problem of religious establishment by separating church and state. The consistent conclusion—drawn by scholars such as Tamara Metz in Untying the Knot—is that we must now separate marriage and state, and for exactly the same reason.

If neutrality were not enough, the historical record alone should disqualify the state as the steward of our intimate lives. Government control of marriage has been, almost without interruption, an instrument of oppression. Under the common-law doctrine of coverture, marriage was the device by which a wife's legal personhood was extinguished—her property, her wages, and her very identity absorbed into her husband's. States weaponized the marriage license to enforce racial caste: sixteen states still banned interracial marriage when the Supreme Court finally intervened in Loving v. Virginia in 1967, and many more had done so earlier. In the eugenics era, states denied marriage licenses to the "feeble-minded" and demanded medical certificates certifying eugenic fitness; well into the twentieth century, couples submitted to mandatory blood tests as a condition of the government's blessing. Several states continued to criminalize the mere cohabitation of unmarried couples into the twenty-first century. An institution with this record has not earned the right to define love. It has forfeited it.

Consider, too, what decades of culture war have actually been about. The long, bitter struggle over same-sex marriage—ballot initiatives, constitutional amendments, litigation culminating in Obergefell v. Hodges—was at bottom a struggle over who controls the government's stamp of approval. Each side fought to capture the state definition because the state definition was the prize. The same dynamic fuels today's skirmishes over officiants, licenses, and religious exemptions. There is a word for a political system in which rival factions must perpetually battle to seize control of the official definition of intimacy: establishment. And there is a well-tested solution: disestablishment. If the state defined nothing, there would be nothing to capture. Same-sex couples, plural families, celibate companions, and traditional believers would each order their unions according to their own convictions, in their own communities, without asking a legislature to ratify their worth. Disestablishment is not a threat to religious marriage; it is religious marriage's liberation, returning the sacrament entirely to the churches that claim it.

The egalitarian case is equally powerful. Legal marriage is not merely a definition; it is a bundle of privilege. By the Government Accountability Office's 2004 count, 1,138 federal statutory provisions turn on marital status—touching taxation, inheritance, Social Security, immigration, hospital access, bereavement leave, and more—quite apart from thousands of state provisions. Every one of these provisions discriminates. It discriminates against the single person who pays more tax on the same income; against the two elderly sisters who have shared a home and cared for one another for fifty years yet may not inherit as spouses do; against the devoted friend who nursed a dying companion for a decade and receives nothing, while a spouse of nine months collects survivor benefits; against the immigrant whose lifelong partner does not fit the government's categories. Before marriage equality, this machinery barred untold numbers of partners from hospital bedsides altogether. The deeper scandal is not that this or that group was excluded from the privileged status. It is that the state maintains a privileged status of intimacy at all—a hierarchy in which one form of love, certified by the county clerk, buys advantages that no amount of devotion, care, or commitment can otherwise obtain. A government of equals has no business ranking its citizens' hearts.

Defenders of the status quo often concede the unfairness but insist the bundle is administratively necessary. This gets things exactly backwards. Marriage is the only contract in the legal system whose terms are never shown to the parties. Couples sign nothing; they are handed no document enumerating the thousand-plus obligations they are assuming; most could not name a dozen of them. It is a one-size-fits-all legal straitjacket imposed on the most diverse institution in human life, and it is the only relationship a person cannot leave without petitioning a judge for permission—the state is, quite literally, the third party to every marriage, and its consent is required for divorce. Nothing about this is protective. It is paternalism masquerading as protection, and it serves mainly to generate litigation over who counts as married, under which state's rules, retroactive to when.

The alternative is not chaos but clarity, and its components already exist. The legal functions currently bundled into marriage can be unbundled into four neutral mechanisms. Second, decision-making and inheritance: a universal designation registry would allow any adult to name any person—spouse, sibling, friend, neighbor—for medical decisions, hospital access, inheritance defaults, and bereavement rights, without the state inquiring into the nature of the relationship. Third, children: custody, support, and parental responsibility should flow from parentage, as they already do for the unmarried. Fourth, care: as legal theorist Martha Fineman has long argued, if the state wishes to support the socially vital work of caregiving, it should support caregiving directly—subsidizing the caretaker-and-dependent dyad, whoever comprises it—rather than using sexual-romantic marriage as a clumsy and exclusionary proxy.

The objection that marriage exists for children deserves a direct answer, because it is the strongest one available. Its premise is simply false as a matter of current law. The obligations of parents to children—support, custody, inheritance—already attach to parenthood, not to marriage; the unmarried father owes child support today, and the law long ago abolished the legal disabilities once inflicted on so-called illegitimate children. Marriage is a wretched proxy for children's interests: many married couples have no children, and millions of children are raised by unmarried parents, grandparents, and others whose households the marital regime ignores or penalizes. If children's welfare is the goal, the honest policy is to protect children directly—through robust parentage law, enforcement of support obligations, and support for their caregivers—rather than through a status that correlates only loosely with the thing we actually care about. Nor should we forget the costs of the proxy: the stigma the marital frame has historically inflicted on children born outside it, and the perverse incentives created when benefits vanish if a poor mother marries.

A second objection worries about the economically vulnerable partner—the spouse who leaves the workforce to raise children and would be exposed without marriage's protections. Here again, the defense rests on a romanticized picture of the institution as it actually operates. Since the no-fault revolution, marriage's protections for the dependent spouse have been steadily hollowed out: permanent alimony is now rare, rehabilitative support is short, and a homemaker may be dismissed from a decades-long marriage with little more than an equitable division of assets the marriage never accumulated. The contract regime proposed here can do better precisely because its terms are real: negotiated provisions for career sacrifice, compensation clauses reviewed with independent advice, default property-sharing rules that attach to long-term cohabiting economic partnerships whether or not anyone signs anything, and doctrines like unjust enrichment—which courts have applied to unmarried partners since Marvin v. Marvin—as a backstop. The license demands no disclosure, no counseling, no comprehension. A system of informed contract would demand all three.

The remaining objections are practical and expressive, and both fail. Practically, abolition simplifies rather than complicates: it ends litigation over common-law marriage, over the validity of foreign unions, over who is "really" married; it ends the degrading spectacle of immigration officials interviewing couples separately about their bedrooms and breakfast habits to detect "marriage fraud"; it ends the federal government's unedifying experiments in marriage promotion, on which hundreds of millions of welfare dollars have been spent with evaluations finding scant effect. Other jurisdictions can recognize private contracts and designations by the ordinary principles of comity that already govern cross-border legal relations. As for the expressive objection—that people want the state's recognition—this deserves to be named for what it is: the deepest symptom of the disease. That free people should crave a bureaucrat's blessing on their love shows how thoroughly the state has colonized intimate life. Recognition that matters comes from family, friends, congregation, and community. The government's approval is worth precisely what the government's disapproval is worth: nothing that a free society should traffic in.

Marriage is too important to be left to the state—too sacred for believers to want it licensed, too varied to be forced into a single statutory mold, too intimate to be rationed by clerks, and too historically abused by governments to be entrusted to them now. The reform proposed here asks no one to surrender anything real: not their vows, not their ceremonies, not their faith's teachings, not their legal security. It asks only that the government exit the wedding chapel, repeal the thousand statutes that sort citizens by marital status, and treat every adult's relationships with equal indifference and equal respect. A promise made before one's family, one's friends, or one's God requires no permission slip from the county. The law should govern our contracts and protect our children; it should leave our loves alone. Love needs no license.
