Marriage Should Be Private: The Case for Removing It from the Legal Sphere

Marriage is often described as a sacred bond, a social institution, a romantic commitment, a religious covenant, or a lifelong partnership. It may be any or all of these things. What it should not be, however, is a legal status conferred, defined, licensed, and privileged by the state.

The government should neither authorize marriages nor prohibit them. It should not decide which relationships count as marriages, impose a standard package of rights and obligations on married people, or make access to taxes, inheritance, health care, immigration, and other legal benefits depend on whether someone has entered a state-approved intimate relationship. Marriage should be removed entirely from the legal sphere and returned to the individuals, families, communities, and religious traditions that give it meaning.

This does not mean abolishing commitment, weddings, families, or enforceable agreements between partners. It means abolishing civil marriage as a government-created status. Adults should remain free to call themselves married, hold ceremonies, exchange vows, follow religious rules, and sign private contracts governing property, support, caregiving, and separation. The state’s role should be limited to enforcing valid agreements, protecting children and vulnerable people, preventing coercion and fraud, and applying general laws equally to everyone.

Such a system would protect freedom of conscience, promote equality, reduce arbitrary legal privilege, and make family law more honest and adaptable.

The State Has No Legitimate Authority to Define Marriage

Marriage has no single universally accepted meaning. For some people, it is a sacrament instituted by God. For others, it is a secular expression of romantic love. Some understand it as a permanent union; others accept divorce. Some view it primarily as a framework for raising children, while others marry without intending or being able to have children. Different cultures and religious traditions disagree about ceremonies, obligations, gender roles, sexual exclusivity, and the conditions under which a marriage begins or ends.

When the state legally defines marriage, it inevitably selects among these competing conceptions. Even a broad and inclusive definition remains an official government definition. The law thereby turns a deeply personal and often religious institution into a public license.

That is unnecessary and inappropriate. Governments do not issue licenses declaring friendships valid. They do not certify religious conversions, approve godparent relationships, or decide which communities may recognize someone as a spiritual leader. The state may regulate conduct when necessary to protect rights, but it should not decide the meaning of intimate or sacred bonds.

Removing marriage from the law would allow every person and community to define it according to conscience. A church could recognize marriages under its doctrine. A secular organization could offer its own ceremonies and standards. Individuals could create new forms of commitment without seeking government approval. No group would be forced to change its beliefs, and no group could use the state to impose those beliefs on others.

This is genuine pluralism: not a single official definition broad enough to include everyone, but no official definition at all.

Legal Marriage Creates Arbitrary Inequality

Civil marriage does more than acknowledge affection. It distributes a large package of legal and economic advantages. Depending on the jurisdiction, marriage can affect taxation, inheritance, pensions, insurance, medical decision-making, property ownership, immigration, government benefits, testimonial privileges, and liability for debts.

Tying these consequences to marriage is arbitrary.

Why should two romantic partners receive tax treatment unavailable to two siblings who share a home and care for each other? Why should a spouse automatically have greater hospital access than a lifelong friend who is the patient’s actual caregiver? Why should immigration law favor a newly married couple over other families facing separation? Why should a person’s eligibility for public benefits depend on whether the government classifies an intimate partner’s income as part of the household?

The usual answer is that marriage signals commitment and interdependence. But it is an unreliable proxy for both. Some married couples keep their finances and daily lives largely separate. Some unmarried partners share everything. Friends, siblings, extended relatives, and caregiving networks may be far more interdependent than many spouses. A legal system that privileges marriage mistakes one culturally favored relationship form for the full range of human dependency.

This privilege also pressures people to marry for legal reasons rather than personal ones. Couples may marry to obtain health insurance, immigration status, tax advantages, or authority during a medical emergency. In such cases, the state is not merely recognizing a private commitment; it is financially and legally steering people toward a particular status.

Equality requires a different approach. Rights should attach to individuals, actual responsibilities, or explicit legal designations—not to a government-approved romantic category.

Abolition Would Better Protect Freedom of Conscience

State marriage continually generates conflicts because it combines two fundamentally different things: a personal or religious institution and a civil status. Once the government calls a legal relationship “marriage,” disputes naturally arise over who must recognize, facilitate, or celebrate it.

These conflicts cannot be fully resolved by repeatedly revising the legal definition. Each definition will satisfy some citizens and violate the convictions of others. The durable solution is institutional separation.

Just as religious organizations may define their own doctrines without controlling civil citizenship, private communities should be able to define marriage without controlling legal rights. A religious body could refuse to solemnize a union contrary to its teachings, but that refusal would have no effect on the parties’ ability to enter enforceable contracts. Conversely, a couple would not need permission from a religious institution—or from the state—to describe themselves as married.

This arrangement would protect both sides. Traditional communities would retain authority over their ceremonies and membership rules. Unconventional families would be free to establish their own relationships without asking the government to validate them. The state would remain neutral because it would no longer decide which unions deserve the title.

Government neutrality does not mean suppressing marriage. It means allowing marriage to flourish as a private institution rather than nationalizing it as a legal one.

Private Contracts Can Handle Adult Relationships More Honestly

Critics often assume that abolishing civil marriage would leave partners without legal protection. That need not happen. Most of the practical matters currently bundled into marriage can be addressed through private contracts and simple legal designations.

Adults could create agreements covering:

  • ownership and division of property;
  • responsibility for shared debts;
  • financial support during or after a relationship;
  • inheritance;
  • life insurance and retirement beneficiaries;
  • medical visitation and decision-making;
  • authority to manage affairs during incapacity;
  • duties concerning caregiving;
  • procedures for mediation, arbitration, or separation.

Standardized templates could make these arrangements inexpensive and accessible. Couples who wanted a familiar package could select a comprehensive domestic partnership contract. Others could tailor agreements to their circumstances. People could revise their arrangements as their lives changed rather than remaining bound to a one-size-fits-all status defined by statute.

This would be more honest than current marriage law. Many people enter legal marriage without understanding the obligations it creates. They may view their wedding vows as the substance of the commitment while remaining unaware that the state has imposed complex rules regarding assets, debts, support, and dissolution. The resulting “contract” is often neither read nor negotiated.

A true contractual system would require clearer consent. Partners would know which rights and responsibilities they were assuming. Expectations would be stated rather than presumed. Disputes could be resolved by reference to the parties’ actual commitments, subject to ordinary safeguards against coercion, fraud, exploitation, and unconscionable terms.

Not every detail should be freely negotiable. The law should continue to prohibit abuse, enforce minimum labor and welfare protections where relevant, and refuse agreements produced by force or deception. But these are general protections of persons, not reasons to maintain civil marriage.

Children Do Not Require Legal Marriage

The most serious objection is that marriage protects children and family stability. Children do need protection, but civil marriage is neither necessary nor sufficient to provide it.

Parental obligations should arise from parenthood and caregiving, not from the marital status of adults. Every child should have equal rights to financial support, care, safety, inheritance protections, and legal recognition of responsible parents regardless of whether those parents married, remained together, or ever had a romantic relationship.

The law should therefore regulate parent-child relationships directly. It should establish parentage through birth, adoption, acknowledgment, or adjudication. It should require responsible parents to support their children. It should determine custody according to the child’s welfare and protect children against abuse and neglect. None of these functions requires the state to recognize a marriage between adults.

Indeed, tying children’s security to marriage historically stigmatized those born outside it and created unequal categories of legitimacy. A child should never have fewer protections because adults did not obtain a license.

Family stability is valuable, but legal privilege is a poor way to create it. A marriage certificate cannot produce love, patience, responsibility, or safety. It cannot prevent abandonment or abuse. Stable families are built through conduct and commitment, not terminology. Law should protect children from harmful conduct and enforce actual duties rather than presuming that married households are virtuous and unmarried households defective.

Divorce Shows the Weakness of the Current Model

Civil marriage is often defended as a stabilizing commitment, yet the state also maintains an elaborate system for dissolving it. Divorce courts must divide property, assign debts, determine support, and sometimes interpret expectations that were never clearly expressed. The process can be expensive, adversarial, and emotionally destructive.

A contractual approach would not eliminate painful separations, but it could reduce uncertainty. Partners could agree in advance on property ownership, financial obligations, and methods of dispute resolution. Courts would intervene primarily when agreements were unclear, invalid, exploitative, or inconsistent with independent duties toward children.

This would also remove the misleading fiction that all married couples have entered essentially the same relationship. They have not. Some merge every asset; others do not. Some expect one partner to leave paid employment; others insist on economic independence. Some intend a permanent commitment regardless of hardship; others accept separation under specified conditions. The law currently imposes default rules while allowing people to project radically different expectations onto the same status.

Explicit agreements would encourage difficult but necessary conversations. What do the partners owe each other? How will they handle sacrificed career opportunities? Who owns what? What happens if one becomes disabled? What responsibilities survive separation? These questions should be answered through informed consent, not hidden within a ceremonial “yes.”

Public Benefits Should Be Individualized or Based on Actual Dependency

Abolishing legal marriage would require reform beyond family law. Governments would need to stop using marital status as a shortcut in taxation and public benefits.

That would be an advantage, not a flaw.

Taxes should ordinarily be assessed on individuals. If the government wishes to recognize dependents, caregiving, disability, or child-rearing expenses, it should do so directly. Benefits should be based on need and actual responsibility. Survivor benefits should follow designated beneficiaries or demonstrable dependency. Medical decision-making should follow the patient’s recorded choices, with neutral fallback rules when no designation exists.

Immigration presents a harder issue because family reunification policies commonly rely on marriage. Yet marriage is already an imperfect and manipulable proxy for genuine attachment. A fairer system could allow sponsorship through clearly defined commitments, dependency, caregiving relationships, or designated close-family bonds. Fraud prevention would remain legitimate, but it would focus on false claims and evasion rather than policing whether a relationship conforms to an official romantic model.

The transition would require careful legislation. Administrative inconvenience, however, is not a principled defense of inequality. Governments frequently use crude categories because they are easy to administer. That does not make them just.

Abolition Would Not Privatize Abuse or Eliminate Protection

Another objection is that removing marriage from law would leave economically vulnerable partners—especially those who perform unpaid domestic labor—without protection.

This concern is important, but it supports stronger general protections rather than civil marriage. Existing marriage law does not reliably protect vulnerable people. Some are pressured into marriage, trapped by financial dependency, or harmed by rules that assume consent where little practical choice exists. Others devote years to caregiving without marrying and receive no comparable protection at all.

The law should address vulnerability directly. Courts should enforce agreements for support and compensation. Legislatures could recognize claims based on detrimental reliance, unjust enrichment, shared enterprises, or uncompensated caregiving. People who sacrifice income to care for children or dependent adults should have protections based on that work, whether they are spouses, partners, relatives, or friends.

Domestic violence laws must apply regardless of marital status. Sexual assault should never be excused by a relationship. Protective orders, emergency housing, child-safety measures, and access to justice should depend on danger and abuse, not on whether the victim and perpetrator possess a marriage certificate.

The abolition of civil marriage is not the abolition of law within private life. It is the replacement of status-based regulation with conduct-based protection.

The State Should Enforce Rights, Not Bestow Social Approval

Some defenders of civil marriage argue that public recognition dignifies relationships and expresses social respect. But dignity granted by the state is always accompanied by the power to withhold dignity. If government recognition is what makes a relationship legitimate, then unrecognized relationships become officially inferior.

The state should not be in the business of awarding prestige to private bonds. Its task is to protect liberty, enforce obligations, and secure equal rights.

People do not need government approval for their love to be real. Religious believers do not need a civil license for their covenant to be sacred. Secular partners do not need a statute for their commitment to be meaningful. What people may need are enforceable contracts, protection from abuse, recognized parental responsibilities, and reliable control over property and medical decisions. Those needs can and should be met without transforming marriage into a legal identity.

The distinction is crucial. Legal recognition of specific rights is not the same as legal recognition of marriage. A person may designate a medical proxy without the state declaring the relationship a marriage. Two people may jointly own a home without being spouses. A parent may owe child support without ever having married. A caregiver may receive compensation or inheritance without fitting a romantic category.

The law can recognize facts, agreements, and responsibilities while remaining silent about the cultural meaning of the relationship.

A Practical Transition Is Possible

Ending civil marriage would require a responsible transition rather than the sudden erasure of existing rights. Current marriages could be converted into standardized civil contracts preserving the parties’ existing property and support expectations. People could opt to modify those contracts over time. Existing parental rights and obligations would remain intact because they would be grounded independently in parentage.

Future couples would no longer apply for marriage licenses. Instead, they could register particular legal instruments if they wished: co-ownership agreements, beneficiary designations, powers of attorney, support contracts, and parenting arrangements. Registration could provide public notice where necessary without certifying a marriage.

Government forms would replace “married” and “single” with questions relevant to the matter at hand: Who owns this property? Who is financially dependent on whom? Who is authorized to make medical decisions? Who has responsibility for this child? Who is the designated beneficiary?

Religious and secular organizations could continue issuing marriage certificates, performing ceremonies, and maintaining their own membership records. These certificates would carry personal and communal meaning but no automatic legal package.

The result would not be chaos. It would be legal precision.

Conclusion

Civil marriage is an inherited fusion of private intimacy, religious tradition, economic regulation, and government privilege. Its familiarity makes it appear indispensable, but its functions can be separated and handled more fairly.

The state should protect children, enforce voluntary agreements, punish abuse, prevent fraud, and provide neutral rules for property, dependency, and incapacity. It should not license love, define sacred bonds, privilege romantic couples over other forms of care, or make basic legal rights depend on membership in a favored relationship category.

Removing marriage from the legal sphere would not weaken marriage. It would liberate it. Marriage could belong fully to those who practice it: to couples, families, faiths, cultures, and communities. It could carry whatever meaning they freely give it, without government endorsement or interference.

At the same time, the law would become more equal. It would address people as individuals, caregivers, parents, property owners, dependents, and contracting parties rather than sorting them into the simplistic categories of married and unmarried.

A free society does not need the state to tell its citizens which intimate relationships are valid. It needs the state to respect their choices, protect their rights, and hold them to the obligations they actually undertake. Marriage should therefore cease to be a legal status and become what it has always been at its core: a private human commitment.

1. Recognition creates coercion, not freedom

To abolish state recognition is not to deny that people may choose marriage. It is to remove the pressure that flows from government endorsement. When the state grants marriage a special status—along with legal benefits, social legitimacy, and administrative procedures—it creates a powerful incentive for individuals to conform. Even when people claim they are choosing freely, the surrounding legal environment shapes what “free choice” looks like in practice.

A private model reverses that dynamic: if people want rights, responsibilities, protections, and procedures, they can secure them through private agreements and general legal mechanisms that do not single out one form of intimacy for state privileging. Even if a society professes neutrality between different relationship forms, state marriage regimes inevitably privilege certain configurations. They do so not only through direct rules (eligibility, grounds for dissolution, and presumptions about parenthood) but through the architecture of civil life that depends on marital status.

This creates a category problem: the state designates certain relationships as “real” and others as “unrecognized,” even when the lived bonds are identical in commitment, interdependence, or caregiving. In practice, people who choose not to marry—or who cannot marry—often face higher transaction costs, uncertainty, and unequal access to remedies.

3. The state’s role in marriage invites regulation of intimacy

Marriage law is not limited to recognizing a couple; it governs the relationship’s lifecycle. The state’s involvement shapes how people behave within their intimate lives. This can appear in obvious ways—such as divorce procedures, legal presumptions about spousal duties, and restrictions that dictate what counts as a valid marriage—but also in subtle ones, such as the allocation of legal responsibilities in ways that treat partners as a unit whose internal dynamics the law can recognize, infer, and override.

When the state regulates marriage, it assumes authority over the boundaries of intimate life: who counts as a spouse, when the relationship ends, what legal effects follow from commitment, and how those effects should be administered. Even if most regulations are framed as protecting stability or preventing harm, the deeper problem remains: intimacy becomes a domain where government claims interpretive power.

A private model strips intimacy of legal mystique. If adults want to define their rights and responsibilities, they can do so through contract, property arrangements, healthcare directives, and—critically—through child-centered legal rules that focus on parenting rather than on conjugal status.

One of the strongest arguments for abolition is that marriage’s legal functions are not unique. Most of what marriage law claims to accomplish—property management, inheritance defaults, decision-making authority during incapacity, insurance coordination, and inheritance rights—can be achieved through general legal tools.

The extensive government regulation of marriage is a relatively recent phenomenon, emerging primarily in the 19th and 20th centuries. Employer-provided benefits often extend to spouses but not to other important relationships, creating arbitrary distinctions that may not reflect the reality of people's lives.

Protecting Children Without Government Marriage

Critics often argue that government must regulate marriage to protect children. This argument fails on multiple levels. The Case for the Complete Abolition of State-Recognized Marriage

Introduction

For centuries, marriage has been a cornerstone of social and legal institutions, governed by religious doctrine, cultural tradition, and state enforcement. However, the modern world has evolved in ways that render state-recognized marriage obsolete, unnecessary, and even harmful. The legal regulation of marriage—whether through licensing, tax benefits, or legal protections—is an outdated relic of a time when the state had a vested interest in controlling reproductive and economic relationships. Today, marriage serves no legitimate public purpose, imposes arbitrary restrictions on personal freedom, and perpetuates systemic inequalities. The only rational and just solution is the complete abolition of state recognition and regulation of marriage, reducing it to a purely private relationship or contract, free from government interference.

This essay will argue that state-recognized marriage is:

  1. An unnecessary and inefficient government function that could be replaced by private contracts and civil unions.
  2. A tool of social control that enforces outdated moral and religious norms, restricting individual autonomy.
  3. A source of systemic inequality, favoring certain relationships over others while excluding those who do not conform to traditional definitions.
  4. A financial and administrative burden on taxpayers, with minimal public benefit.
  5. A relic of patriarchal and property-based legal systems that no longer aligns with modern values of personal liberty and equality.

By removing marriage from the legal sphere, society would achieve greater freedom, fairness, and efficiency—allowing individuals to define their relationships on their own terms, free from state coercion.

I. Marriage as an Unnecessary and Inefficient Government Function

One of the strongest arguments for abolishing state-recognized marriage is that it serves no essential public function that cannot be fulfilled by private agreements. The state’s involvement in marriage is a holdover from feudal and religious legal systems, where marriage was a means of regulating property, inheritance, and social order. Today, however, the functions traditionally performed by marriage—such as inheritance rights, tax benefits, and medical decision-making—can be achieved through private contracts, wills, and civil unions without the need for state intervention.

A. Private Contracts Can Replace Marriage Licenses

The primary legal benefits of marriage—such as spousal inheritance rights, tax exemptions, and medical decision-making authority—are not inherent to marriage itself but rather legal privileges granted by the state. These same protections can be secured through:

  • Co-habitation agreements (covering property, finances, and inheritance)
  • Medical power of attorney (allowing individuals to designate decision-makers)
  • Joint tenancy or community property agreements (ensuring financial rights)
  • Life insurance policies and beneficiary designations (securing financial support)

If two people wish to formalize their commitment, they can do so through private vows, religious ceremonies, or legally binding contracts—without requiring government approval. The state’s role in marriage is purely bureaucratic, adding unnecessary red tape to what should be a personal matter.

B. Civil Unions Already Prove Marriage Is Redundant

Many jurisdictions already offer civil unions or domestic partnerships, which provide the same legal benefits as marriage without the symbolic or religious connotations. If the state’s only concern is ensuring that committed couples have legal protections, then civil unions are a far more efficient and neutral solution than marriage. They avoid the moral and political controversies surrounding marriage while still fulfilling the supposed "public interest" in stable relationships.

The fact that civil unions exist at all proves that marriage is not a necessary legal institution—it is merely a social and historical tradition that the state has chosen to privilege over other forms of commitment.

C. The Administrative Burden of Marriage Licensing

Marriage licensing is an expensive and time-consuming process that serves no clear public good. Governments spend millions on:

  • Issuing and processing marriage licenses (clerks, paperwork, fees)
  • Enforcing marriage laws (bigamy prosecutions, divorce proceedings)
  • Maintaining marriage records (which are rarely needed for anything beyond inheritance disputes)

These resources could be redirected to more pressing public needs—such as healthcare, education, or infrastructure—if the state simply stopped regulating marriage entirely.

Conclusion: Since private contracts and civil unions can replicate all the legal benefits of marriage, the state’s involvement in marriage is unnecessary, inefficient, and wasteful.

II. Marriage as a Tool of Social Control and Moral Coercion

Beyond its bureaucratic inefficiency, state-recognized marriage is a mechanism of social control, enforcing moral and religious norms that have no place in a secular, liberal democracy. The state’s definition of marriage has historically been used to:

  • Police sexual morality (e.g., banning same-sex marriage, criminalizing interracial marriage)
  • Enforce gender roles (e.g., requiring a "husband" and "wife" designation)
  • Discourage alternative lifestyles (e.g., penalizing cohabitation outside marriage)

Even today, marriage remains tied to outdated religious and cultural expectations, despite the fact that personal relationships should be a matter of individual choice, not state approval.

A. The State Should Not Impose Moral Judgments on Relationships

Marriage has long been used as a tool to enforce religious doctrine. For example:

  • Christian marriage laws historically required religious ceremonies and prohibited divorce.
  • Sharia law in some countries mandates polygyny and gender segregation in marriage.
  • Anti-miscegenation laws (banning interracial marriage) were justified under the guise of "protecting marriage."

Even in modern secular states, marriage laws reflect cultural biases—such as:

  • The "one man, one woman" definition, which excludes polyamorous, queer, and non-monogamous relationships.
  • The assumption that marriage is permanent, despite high divorce rates.
  • The financial incentives for marriage, which pressure people into traditional family structures.

A truly neutral state should not dictate who can or cannot marry—or what form their commitment should take. If two (or more) consenting adults wish to formalize their relationship, they should be free to do so without government interference.

B. Marriage Perpetuates Gender Inequality

Historically, marriage was a legal contract that subjugated women to male authority. Even today, many marriage laws reinforce patriarchal structures, such as:

  • Prenuptial agreements (which often favor husbands in property disputes)
  • Alimony laws (which can financially penalize women after divorce)
  • Default inheritance rules (which may leave widows vulnerable if not properly planned)

While some of these issues can be addressed through private contracts, the fact that marriage default settings often disadvantage women shows that state-recognized marriage is not a neutral institution.

C. The State Has No Legitimate Interest in Private Relationships

The only justification for state involvement in marriage is the supposed "public interest" in stable families. However:

  • Not all stable relationships are marriages (e.g., long-term cohabitation, polyamorous households).
  • Not all marriages are stable (divorce rates are high, and many married couples are unhappy).
  • The state has no business arbitrating personal happiness or commitment.

If the goal is social stability, then the state should focus on providing social services, education, and economic support—not regulating who can love whom.

Conclusion: Marriage is not a neutral legal institution but a tool of moral and social control. A free society should remove marriage from the legal sphere and allow individuals to define their relationships without state interference.

III. Marriage as a Source of Systemic Inequality

One of the most damaging aspects of state-recognized marriage is its exclusionary nature. By defining marriage in a narrow, traditional way, the state creates a legal hierarchy of relationships, where some are privileged and others are marginalized. This leads to systemic inequality in:

  • Legal rights (e.g., unmarried couples lack spousal benefits)
  • Tax and inheritance laws (e.g., married couples get favorable treatment)
  • Social recognition (e.g., only married couples are socially validated)

A. Marriage Creates a Two-Tiered Legal System

Under current laws, married couples enjoy automatic legal protections that unmarried couples must fight for through complex legal workarounds. For example:

  • Medical decision-making: A spouse can automatically make medical decisions for an incapacitated partner, while an unmarried partner may be legally barred from doing so without a power of attorney.
  • Inheritance rights: A spouse inherits automatically, while an unmarried partner may be disinherited if not properly documented.
  • Tax benefits: Married couples receive lower tax rates, estate tax exemptions, and social security benefits, while unmarried couples must pay more and jump through bureaucratic hoops to access the same privileges.

This two-tiered system is unjust and inefficient. If the state’s goal is to ensure that committed couples have legal protections, then all committed couples should have equal access to those protections—regardless of whether they call themselves "married."

B. Marriage Excludes Non-Traditional Relationships

The traditional definition of marriage excludes many valid and stable relationships, including:

  • Polyamorous relationships (where multiple partners are committed to each other)
  • Queer and non-monogamous relationships (which may not fit the "husband-wife" model)
  • Long-term cohabiting couples (who may not wish to marry but still need legal protections)
  • Single parents and chosen families (who form deep bonds outside marriage)

By only recognizing one form of commitment, the state erases the legitimacy of other relationships, leading to legal vulnerabilities for those who do not fit the mold.

C. The "Marriage Penalty" Hurts Low-Income and Unmarried Couples

Ironically, marriage often benefits the wealthy more than the poor. For example:

  • Wealthy couples can use marriage to minimize taxes, pass down wealth, and secure inheritance.
  • Low-income couples may lose welfare benefits if they marry (due to asset tests).
  • Unmarried couples (especially same-sex couples in some states) face higher costs for healthcare, housing, and legal protections.

This regressive system punishes the poor and marginalized while rewarding the already privileged. A truly equitable system would decouple legal benefits from marriage and instead provide universal protections for all committed relationships.

Conclusion: State-recognized marriage creates arbitrary legal hierarchies, excludes non-traditional relationships, and disproportionately harms the poor and marginalized. The only fair solution is to abolish marriage as a legal category and replace it with universal relationship protections.

IV. Marriage as a Financial and Administrative Burden

Beyond its moral and legal problems, state-recognized marriage is a costly and bureaucratic system that drains public resources without providing sufficient benefits. The financial and administrative burdens of marriage include:

A. The Cost of Marriage Licensing and Enforcement

Governments spend millions annually on:

  • Issuing and processing marriage licenses (clerks, paperwork, fees)
  • Maintaining marriage records (which are rarely accessed except in legal disputes)
  • Enforcing marriage laws (bigamy prosecutions, divorce proceedings, alimony disputes)

These costs could be eliminated if marriage were removed from the legal system.

B. The Taxpayer Subsidy for Marriage

The government heavily subsidizes marriage through:

  • Tax breaks for married couples (lower tax rates, estate tax exemptions)
  • Social Security benefits for spouses
  • Healthcare and insurance benefits for dependents

These subsidies favor married couples over unmarried ones, creating unfair economic advantages based on marital status rather than need.

If the goal is to support families, then universal childcare, healthcare, and economic assistance would be far more effective than marriage-specific benefits.

C. The Divorce Industry: A Self-Perpetuating Bureaucracy

Divorce is one of the most lucrative (and painful) industries in the legal system. Millions are spent annually on:

  • Divorce lawyers
  • Court fees
  • Child custody battles
  • Property disputes

If marriage were not a legal institution, divorce would cease to exist as a legal process, saving billions in legal fees and court costs.

Conclusion: Marriage is an expensive and inefficient system that wastes taxpayer money on bureaucracy, subsidies, and legal disputes. Removing it from the legal sphere would save money, reduce litigation, and eliminate unfair economic privileges.

V. Marriage as a Relic of Patriarchal and Property-Based Law

Finally, state-recognized marriage is a holdover from feudal and property-based legal systems, where women were legal property and relationships were economic transactions. While modern marriage has evolved, its legal foundations remain rooted in outdated assumptions about:

  • Gender roles (the "breadwinner-homemaker" model)
  • Property rights (marriage as a way to transfer wealth)
  • Reproductive control (marriage as a way to regulate sex and childbirth)

A. Marriage Was Originally a Property Transaction

In Roman law, common law, and religious doctrine, marriage was a contract between families to:

  • Transfer dowries and inheritances
  • Secure male control over women’s bodies and labor
  • Legitimize children for inheritance purposes

Even today, marriage laws reflect these old assumptions, such as:

  • The "fault" divorce system (where one spouse is blamed for the breakdown)
  • Alimony laws (which often assume the wife was financially dependent)
  • Paternity laws (which assume the husband is the automatic father of his wife’s children)

B. The State Should Not Enforce Gender Norms

Marriage reinforces traditional gender roles by:

  • Assuming a "husband" and "wife" dynamic (even in same-sex marriages)
  • Providing financial incentives for heterosexual nuclear families
  • Disadvantaging single parents, cohabiting couples, and non-traditional families

A truly egalitarian legal system would not tie benefits to marital status but instead provide universal support for all caring relationships.

C. Reproductive Freedom Should Not Depend on Marriage

Historically, marriage was a way to control women’s sexuality and reproduction. Even today, many legal benefits (such as maternity leave, adoption rights, and medical decision-making) are tied to marriage, forcing women into dependent relationships to access basic rights.

If the goal is reproductive justice, then marriage should not be a prerequisite for parental rights, healthcare, or economic stability.

Conclusion: Marriage is a legal relic of patriarchal and property-based systems that no longer aligns with modern values of equality and autonomy. The only logical step is to dismantle it entirely and replace it with private contracts and universal relationship protections.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Objection 1: "Without marriage, society will lack stability."

Rebuttal: Society does not need marriage to function. Stability comes from economic security, education, and social support—not legal marriage. Rebuttal: They would gain them. Instead of only married couples getting automatic rights, all committed couples could access the same protections through private contracts. This would eliminate the two-tiered legal system and ensure fairness for everyone.

Conclusion: The Case for a Marriage-Free Society

State-recognized marriage is an outdated, inefficient, and unjust institution that serves no legitimate public purpose. It is:

  • Unnecessary, since private contracts and civil unions can replace all its legal functions.
  • Oppressive, as it enforces moral and religious norms on personal relationships.
  • Inequitable, as it creates legal hierarchies that disadvantage the poor, unmarried, and non-traditional couples.
  • Expensive, wasting taxpayer money on bureaucracy, subsidies, and divorce litigation.
  • Patriarchal, rooted in old property laws that no longer reflect modern values.

The only rational solution is to completely abolish state recognition and regulation of marriage, reducing it to a purely private relationship or contract. This would: ✅ Free individuals from state coercion in their personal lives. ✅ Eliminate legal discrimination against unmarried and non-traditional couples. ✅ Save taxpayer money by removing an unnecessary bureaucratic system. ✅ Promote true equality by treating all committed relationships the same. ✅ Align the law with modern values of autonomy, diversity, and personal freedom.

Beyond the State's Authority: A Case for the Complete Abolition of State-Recognized Marriage

Introduction

Few institutions have so thoroughly interwoven themselves with both private life and public law as marriage. For centuries, governments have defined who may marry, under what conditions, with what rights, and with what consequences. Yet a growing intellectual movement—drawing on libertarian, feminist, civil rights, and pragmatic progressive traditions—contends that the very foundation of this arrangement is illegitimate. The argument is not merely that marriage should be reformed, expanded, or made more inclusive, but that the state should withdraw entirely from the business of defining, recognizing, and regulating intimate human relationships. Marriage, in this view, should be removed from the legal sphere and treated as what its advocates claim it truly is: a private relationship, a personal commitment, or at most a private contract between consenting adults.

This essay argues for that position. It is not a moderate position, and it does not pretend to be. The complete abolition of state-recognized marriage is a radical idea, but radicalism is sometimes the only honest response to an institution that has historically combined discriminatory exclusion, religious entanglement, patriarchal subordination, and coercive state power. The following pages will set forth the strongest case for abolition: that state involvement in marriage is philosophically unjustifiable, practically harmful, and inconsistent with the principles of equal liberty that modern democracies claim to uphold.

I. The State Has No Legitimate Authority Over Intimate Relationships

The foundational argument for abolishing state-recognized marriage is the principle that government has no business regulating the private, intimate commitments between consenting adults. A free society, properly understood, draws a line between the public sphere—where the state may legitimately exercise authority—and the private sphere, where individuals must be free to make their own choices about how to live.

Marriage lies squarely within the private sphere. It is, at its core, a declaration of personal commitment, a recognition of emotional and often sexual intimacy, and an arrangement for mutual support and shared life. These are matters of conscience, affection, and personal project—precisely the kinds of decisions that liberal political theory has long held should be insulated from state interference. When the government prescribes who may marry, what ceremonies are valid, what rights flow from marriage, or what obligations couples must accept, it is doing something that exceeds its legitimate authority.

This is not to say that the state has no role in enforcing contracts, protecting people from fraud, or safeguarding the vulnerable. These are legitimate state functions. But the state can perform all of them without maintaining a special legal institution called "marriage" with its bundled package of rights and obligations. Couples—whether romantic, platonic, domestic, or polyamorous—can structure their relationships through ordinary contract law, wills, property arrangements, and other private legal mechanisms. The state's role should be limited to providing neutral legal tools, not to anointing certain relationships as legally privileged.

The current regime, by contrast, is one in which the state has inserted itself into the most personal corner of human life, declaring which relationships count, which don't, and what legal consequences flow from them. This is a profound overreach—one that no other area of private life would tolerate. We do not, for instance, allow the state to recognize and regulate friendships, sibling relationships, or other intimate bonds. The asymmetry is striking, and the only justification for it is tradition and inertia.

II. State Recognition Inevitably Produces Discrimination

A second, more pragmatic argument is that wherever the state draws lines around marriage, those lines will exclude and harm someone. The history of state-regulated marriage is essentially a history of who has been excluded from it: women without property, people of different races, same-sex couples, those deemed mentally or physically "unfit," and countless others whose relationships the state refused to recognize.

Some might respond that we have largely solved this problem by expanding marriage rights—interracial marriage, same-sex marriage, and so on. But this response misunderstands the critique. The argument is not that the current lines are drawn in the wrong place, but that the act of drawing lines at all is the problem. Every line the state draws around marriage creates insiders and outsiders, privileged and unprivileged, recognized and erased.

Consider the practical consequences. Marriage comes with thousands of legal benefits and obligations: tax status, inheritance rights, hospital visitation, immigration privileges, medical decision-making authority, and more. A couple that the state recognizes as married receives an enormous bundle of legal advantages that an unmarried couple—whether they are cohabiting partners, deeply committed but unmarried for personal reasons, or simply philosophically opposed to the institution—does not. This creates a two-tiered system in which the state actively incentivizes and rewards one particular form of relationship while leaving all others in legal limbo.

This is not a bug of the system that can be patched; it is a feature. Any system in which the state recognizes certain relationships as legally privileged will create these tiers, and the people at the bottom of those tiers—whoever they turn out to be in any given era—will bear the burden of the state's moral judgments. The only way to end this cycle of exclusion is to abolish the privileged category altogether.

III. Marriage as a Historically Patriarchal and Unequal Institution

A third line of argument, drawn particularly from feminist thought, holds that state-recognized marriage has been a primary vehicle for women's historical subordination. While modern marriage law has shed some of its most overt patriarchal features, the institution retains a structure that subsidizes and entrenches dependence—particularly women's economic dependence on men.

The "marriage premium" and the "motherhood penalty" are well-documented economic phenomena. Married men tend to earn more; married women, especially mothers, tend to earn less. Marriage, as a state-recognized institution, comes with tax benefits, Social Security spousal benefits, default inheritance arrangements, and other features that incentivize a particular kind of economic arrangement—one in which one partner (historically the wife) sacrifices earning potential to provide unpaid domestic and care work. The state, by subsidizing this arrangement, is effectively paying people to organize their lives in a way that has historically disadvantaged women.

Abolishing state marriage would not mean that couples could not choose this arrangement if they wished. Many would. But it would mean the state would no longer tilt the playing field in favor of this particular model of domestic life. Couples would negotiate their arrangements through private contracts, with full freedom to design relationships based on equality, interdependence, or whatever structure best suited their needs. The default legal structure would not assume or reward the gendered division of labor that has historically defined marriage.

This is not a call to abolish coupledom, romance, or commitment. It is a call to stop having the state enshrine a particular—and historically unequal—model of those things as the legally privileged form of human relationship.

IV. Religious Freedom and the Separation of Powers

A fourth argument concerns the entanglement of state and religious authority. Marriage, as it exists in most contemporary legal systems, is a curious hybrid: a ceremony often performed by religious officials but with legal effects determined by the state. This is no accident. Modern marriage law is a direct descendant of religious canonical law—the Catholic Church's model of marriage as a sacrament governed by ecclesiastical authority was adopted into secular law throughout the Western world during the medieval and early modern periods.

This historical inheritance creates ongoing problems. Religious groups that hold traditional views of marriage—particularly that marriage is between a man and a woman—find themselves in conflict with state law when the state expands marriage to include same-sex couples. Conversely, religious groups or secular individuals who reject the institution altogether find themselves navigating a legal landscape that assumes participation in it. The state, by maintaining a single legal category called "marriage" with substantive content drawn from one religious tradition, is effectively privileging certain theological positions over others.

Abolishing state-recognized marriage would resolve this conflict cleanly. Civil unions, domestic partnerships, or private contracts would handle the legal functions currently performed by marriage. Religious institutions would remain free to perform wedding ceremonies for those who wanted them, but those ceremonies would have no automatic legal effect—any legal consequences would flow from the private arrangements the parties chose to make. Conversely, secular individuals and religious minorities would not be forced to participate in a system that embodies the theological commitments of a tradition they may reject.

This is not a marginal concern. In pluralistic societies with diverse religious and philosophical commitments, the state has no business enforcing a particular conception of marriage. A truly neutral state should leave the definition of marriage to private institutions—religious or otherwise—and concern itself only with the legal arrangements that consenting adults make for themselves.

V. The Contract Model Is Sufficient—and Superior

A common objection to abolishing state-recognized marriage is that marriage performs important social functions—providing certainty, stability, and clarity about the rights and obligations of intimate partners—that could not easily be replicated. But this objection misunderstands what abolition actually entails.

Under an abolitionist framework, marriage as a cultural, religious, and personal institution continues to exist. Couples may still hold wedding ceremonies, exchange vows, declare their commitment publicly, and live together in whatever way they choose. What disappears is the state's recognition of marriage as a special legal status with bundled rights and obligations. In its place, individuals would use ordinary legal tools—contracts, wills, trusts, powers of attorney, healthcare directives, and property agreements—to structure their relationships as they see fit.

This contract model is, in many ways, superior to the current system. Marriage as it exists today is a one-size-fits-all package deal. It assumes a particular kind of relationship—usually two people, often with particular assumptions about sexual exclusivity, economic sharing, and caregiving—and bundles together a fixed set of rights and obligations. Couples who want a different arrangement must either accept the default or hire lawyers to draft elaborate opt-out agreements.

Under a contract model, by contrast, individuals would have far more flexibility to design relationships that actually fit their needs. Two people who want the full traditional package of mutual support and shared property could contract for it. Two people who want to maintain separate property while sharing a home could contract for that. Three or four adults who want to form a polyamorous household could contract for that. People who want to be married in a religious ceremony but maintain legal separation could do so without the awkward legal fictions the current system requires.

The current marriage regime is, in fact, the opposite of what libertarians and progressives alike should want: a state-imposed default that individuals must opt out of, rather than a neutral framework within which individuals can construct the arrangements that suit them.

VI. Anticipating Objections

No argument of this scope can ignore the objections it will face. Several deserve direct response.

The "symbolic" objection. Some argue that marriage has important symbolic value, and that state recognition of it dignifies committed relationships. But the state should not be in the business of dignifying particular forms of human relationship. If anything, the symbolic effect of state recognition is to demean relationships that the state does not recognize—to send a message that some loves, some commitments, some households are more legitimate than others. Abolishing state marriage would symbolically affirm the equal dignity of all caring human relationships.

The "practical benefits" objection. Married couples receive tangible legal benefits—tax advantages, hospital visitation, inheritance, and so on. Abolitionists are not arguing that these benefits should disappear, only that they should be decoupled from marriage. A survivor's Social Security benefit, for example, could be available to any designated beneficiary; hospital visitation rights could be established through simple documents; inheritance could flow through wills. There is no reason these benefits must be tied to marital status.

The "traditional" objection. Marriage is ancient and venerable; surely we should not abolish it. But the institution that exists today bears little resemblance to the marriages of antiquity or the medieval period. Marriage has been continuously transformed—abolishing coverture, adding no-fault divorce, recognizing interracial and same-sex unions, and so on. Abolition would be another transformation, not an attack on commitment or family. It would simply be a recognition that the state should not be the gatekeeper of these intimate arrangements.

The "children" objection. Some argue that marriage stabilizes families and protects children. But the evidence is mixed at best, and what evidence exists suggests that what matters for children is the quality of their caregivers' relationships, not the legal status of those relationships. Moreover, the state's interest in child welfare can be pursued directly through child protection, custody, and support law—without bundling those interests into a marriage regime that also serves adults.

VII. A Vision Beyond Marriage

The abolition of state-recognized marriage is not a minor policy adjustment. It is a fundamental reconsideration of the relationship between the state and the most intimate aspects of human life. It would mean ending a system that has historically excluded, discriminated, and entrenched inequality. It would mean replacing a one-size-fits-all state-imposed default with a flexible framework in which individuals construct their own arrangements. It would mean a clean separation between the state's legitimate functions—enforcing contracts, protecting the vulnerable, ensuring equality under law—and the private choices that define how people love, live, and form households.

This vision is not anti-family, anti-commitment, or anti-love. It is pro-freedom. It trusts adults to make their own choices about their personal lives, and it refuses to allow the state to mark some relationships as more worthy than others. It is the consistent application of principles that liberal democracies already claim to embrace: equal treatment under law, freedom of contract, freedom of conscience, and the limitation of state power over private life.

Marriage, as a private institution, will survive the abolition of state recognition—and it will be stronger for it, no longer distorted by state-imposed definitions and bundled obligations. What will end is the state's role as the official arbiter of which human relationships count. That is an end worth pursuing, and a reform whose time, after centuries of state entanglement, has finally come.

Conclusion

The state should not recognize, define, or regulate marriage. This is not a call to abolish love, commitment, or family, but to stop using the coercive apparatus of the state to enforce a particular model of those goods. Marriage's entanglement with law has produced a long history of exclusion, discrimination, patriarchal subordination, and religious privilege. It has created a two-tiered system in which some relationships are legally elevated while others are erased. It has imposed a one-size-fits-all default on a sphere of life that demands flexibility and respect for individual conscience.

The alternative is a regime in which individuals freely structure their intimate relationships through private contracts and personal arrangements, with the state providing neutral legal infrastructure rather than substantive moral judgments. Such a regime is more equal, more libertarian, more feminist, and more consistent with the principles of a free society than the one we have today.

The complete abolition of state-recognized marriage is a radical proposal, but the institution it would replace is itself a relic of an era when the state claimed authority over nearly every domain of human life. We have long since removed the state from the regulation of religion, from the censorship of speech, and from many other areas of private life. It is past time to do the same for marriage.

Defenders counter that the current system is itself a historical accident that we can redesign to serve the same interests more neutrally.

Abolishing State Marriage: A Case for Privatization

Government interference in personal relationships, particularly through state-sanctioned marriage, infringes upon fundamental freedoms and perpetuates inequality. It is time to critically reassess the state’s role in defining and regulating marriage. A complete separation of marriage from the legal sphere—transforming it into a purely private matter—offers a path toward greater individual autonomy, inclusivity, and legal pragmaticism. This essay advocates for the abolition of state marriage recognition and regulation, arguing that such a transition safeguards liberty, dismantles systemic prejudice, and streamlines legal frameworks to better serve humanity.

I. Violation of Individual Liberty

The state’s involvement in marriage fundamentally violates the principles of individual freedom. By defining marriage’s structure (e.g., monogamy, longevity, gender requirements), governments impose restrictive norms on personal relationships. Even as legal recognition expands to accommodate same-sex unions, the state’s definition remains a one-size-fits-all model that may exclude nontraditional arrangements, such as polyamorous families or committed long-term partnerships. Privatization would allow individuals to craft covenantal agreements tailored to their needs, liberating them from coercive state-imposed expectations. As philosopher Martha Nussbaum argues, “Marriage in a free society should exist only in a private, domestic context,” prioritizing love over law.

II. Elimination of Discriminatory Practices

Historically, marriage laws were tools of discrimination, from banning interracial unions to stigmatizing nonreligious couples. Though progress has been made, traces of inequity linger: immigration policies favor spousal visa sponsorship, and property rights often default to marital status. Abolishing state marriage removes these avenues for systemic bias. Without legal definitions, marginalized relationships—regardless of sexual orientation, race, or belief system—would be immune to exclusion based on institutional criteria. Instead, legal protections could be extended universally through private contracts or alternative frameworks.

The Case for Abolishing State Recognition of Marriage: A Comprehensive Argument

Introduction

For centuries, the institution of marriage has sat at the intersection of law, religion, culture, and personal identity. Governments around the world have woven marriage into the fabric of civil society, conferring upon it a vast array of legal privileges, tax benefits, inheritance rights, and social recognitions. Yet this seemingly natural arrangement raises a profound question that few policymakers have been willing to seriously entertain: Why should the state be in the business of defining, regulating, and privileging a particular form of intimate relationship at all?

This essay argues that the complete removal of marriage from the legal sphere—its abolition as a state-recognized institution—is not only philosophically defensible but practically desirable. Marriage, stripped of its governmental scaffolding, would remain what it has always been at its core: a deeply personal commitment between individuals. What would change is that the state would no longer single out one type of relationship for special treatment, and citizens would gain the freedom to define their own bonds without the coercive supervision of the government.

I. The Historical Case: Marriage as a Tool of State Power

To understand why the state's involvement in marriage should end, it helps to understand how that involvement began. Marriage was not always a civil institution. In ancient Rome, it was primarily a family and religious arrangement. In medieval Europe, the Catholic Church gradually claimed jurisdiction over marriage, and it was only during the Reformation and the rise of the modern nation-state that governments began to systematically regulate it.

The state's interest in marriage has never been neutral. Governments recognized and regulated marriage because it served state purposes:

  1. Population control and demographic engineering. Marriage laws historically incentivized reproduction within a sanctioned framework, ensuring the production of citizens, soldiers, and taxpayers.

  2. Property consolidation and inheritance regulation. Marriage provided a legally predictable mechanism for transferring wealth between generations, benefiting landed aristocracies and, later, the propertied classes.

  3. Social ordering and moral regulation. The state used marriage to enforce racial hierarchies (anti-miscegenation laws), sexual norms (criminalization of adultery, sodomy laws tied to marital definitions), and gender roles (coverture laws that effectively erased a married woman's legal identity).

  4. Economic dependency management. Marriage created a legal obligation for mutual financial support, reducing the likelihood that one partner would become a burden on public welfare systems.

In every era, the state's interest in marriage has been, at bottom, the state's interest in control—over bodies, property, reproduction, and social conformity. Recognizing this history should make us deeply skeptical of the premise that state involvement in marriage is benign, natural, or necessary.

II. The Philosophical Case: Freedom of Association and the Limits of Government

The argument for abolishing state-recognized marriage rests on a simple but powerful liberal principle: the government should not be in the business of defining or privileging personal relationships.

A. The Problem of Definition

Every marriage law requires the state to define what marriage is. This definition inevitably includes some relationships and excludes others. For most of modern history, this meant restricting marriage to heterosexual, monogamous pairs. In recent decades, many nations have expanded the definition to include same-sex couples—rightly so, as a matter of equal treatment.

But the expansion of the definition does not solve the underlying problem; it merely shifts the boundary. Even in jurisdictions with the most inclusive marriage laws, the state still decides:

  • How many people may be married (typically only two).
  • What degree of consanguinity disqualifies a union.
  • What minimum age is acceptable.
  • Whether certain disabilities preclude marriage.
  • Whether mental competency tests should apply.

Why should the state have the authority to answer any of these questions? If three consenting adults wish to commit to one another, on what principled basis does the state tell them they cannot? If two people who happen to be closely related wish to form a domestic partnership without reproducing, why does the state criminalize their union? These are not hypothetical provocations—they are illustrations of how state-defined marriage inevitably imposes a majoritarian moral vision on private life.

The libertarian philosopher Michael Kinsley once observed that the question is not "Should we redefine marriage?" but "Should anyone have the power to define it for others?" Abolishing state-recognized marriage answers this question definitively: no one should.

B. The Problem of Privilege

State-recognized marriage is not merely a label—it is a gateway to a vast array of legal privileges. Married couples receive preferential treatment in:

  • Taxation (joint filing, estate tax exemptions, gift tax exclusions).
  • Immigration (spousal sponsorship and priority visas).
  • Healthcare decision-making (automatic next-of-kin status).
  • Inheritance (intestate succession rights).
  • Insurance and benefits (spousal coverage, Social Security survivor benefits).
  • Parental rights (presumption of paternity, adoption eligibility).
  • Legal protections (spousal privilege in court, domestic violence statutes).

This creates a two-tiered system of citizenship. Those who are married—whether by choice, cultural pressure, or economic necessity—receive a bundle of rights and protections denied to the unmarried. Single individuals, cohabiting partners, close friends who share a household, polyamorous families, elderly siblings who care for one another, and countless other relationship configurations are all systematically disadvantaged.

The state should not reward one form of intimacy over others. A society that values freedom and equality should not offer a legal bonanza to people who happen to conform to a particular relationship model while leaving others to fend for themselves.

C. The Separation of Church (or Culture) and State

For billions of people, marriage is a sacred religious sacrament. For others, it is a cultural tradition, a romantic ideal, or a pragmatic arrangement. By making marriage a civil institution, the state collapses these diverse meanings into a single legal category, inevitably privileging some conceptions over others.

Abolishing state-recognized marriage would actually strengthen the institution of marriage for those who value it. Religious communities would be free to define marriage according to their own doctrines without any governmental interference or redefinition. Cultural groups could maintain their own traditions and ceremonies. The state, for its part, would simply remain silent on the matter—which is precisely where a secular government should stand on questions of personal meaning and spiritual commitment.

III. The Practical Case: A Better System Is Possible

Critics of abolishing state-recognized marriage will immediately object: "But what about all the legal rights and protections that marriage provides? You can't simply eliminate them!"

This objection misunderstands the argument. Abolishing state-recognized marriage does not mean abolishing the legal rights currently bundled into marriage. It means unbundling them—making them available through more flexible, equitable, and voluntary mechanisms.

A. Replacing Marriage with a Civil Partnership or Legal Framework for All

Instead of a single, one-size-fits-all marriage contract, the state could offer a universal civil partnership registration system available to any two (or more) adults who wish to formalize a legal relationship. This system would be:

  • Gender-neutral and configuration-neutral. Any adults could register—friends, siblings, romantic partners, caregivers, etc.
  • Customizable. Registrants could specify the terms of their partnership: shared property arrangements, mutual obligations, healthcare decision-making authority, inheritance terms, and so forth.
  • Scalable. The system would not cap the number of people who could enter into a partnership together, recognizing that families come in many forms.
  • Dissoluble through a clear legal process, much as divorce functions today, but without the moral freight that the word "divorce" carries.

Many of the legal benefits currently reserved for married couples could simply be extended to all individuals or made available through opt-in contracts. For example:

  • Healthcare decision-making: Anyone should be able to designate a healthcare proxy through a simple, standardized legal form—no marriage required.
  • Inheritance: Default intestacy rules could be reformed to better reflect modern family structures, and standardized will templates could be made freely available.
  • Immigration: Sponsorship could be based on demonstrated economic dependency or caregiving relationships, not merely marital status.
  • Taxation: Preferential tax treatment for married couples could be eliminated in favor of individual filing or universal household-based filing.
  • Parental rights: Paternity and maternity could be established through birth registration and voluntary acknowledgment, completely independent of the parents' relationship status.

B. Existing Models and Precedents

Several legal systems already move in this direction, providing proof of concept:

  • France's PACS (Pacte civil de solidarité) offers a registered partnership that is distinct from marriage and available to both same-sex and opposite-sex couples. It confers many (though not all) of the legal rights of marriage with less institutional rigidity.
  • Cohabitation agreements in many common-law jurisdictions allow unmarried partners to define their legal obligations to one another through private contract.
  • Domestic partnership registries in various American cities and states have long offered marriage-like benefits without the marriage label.

The logical endpoint of these developments is clear: the state can provide a framework for formalizing legal obligations between individuals without calling it "marriage" and without limiting it to romantic or sexual partnerships.

C. Addressing the "Bundle of Rights" Concern

Some rights currently tied to marriage are so deeply embedded in legal systems that untangling them will require effort. But effort is not impossibility, and the benefits of reform far outweigh the transitional costs. Consider:

  • Social Security survivor benefits could be restructured as a form of designated beneficiary system, similar to life insurance.
  • Spousal privilege in court could be reframed as a privilege for any person sharing a household or registered partnership.
  • Domestic violence protections are already being extended beyond married couples in most jurisdictions; this trend would simply continue and accelerate.

The key insight is that none of these legal mechanisms require the concept of "marriage" to function. They require the concept of legal relationships between individuals—which is precisely what a reformed system would provide.

IV. The Equality Case: Marriage as Discrimination

State-recognized marriage is, by its very nature, a discriminatory institution. It discriminates in two directions simultaneously:

  1. It discriminates against those who cannot or choose not to marry. Single people, celibate individuals, those who cannot find a partner, those in non-traditional relationship configurations, and those who simply do not wish to marry are all denied a substantial package of legal rights and social recognition.

  2. It discriminates by imposing a single model of intimacy. Even in its most inclusive form, state-recognized marriage privileges dyadic, romantic, sexual relationships above all others. The bond between a parent and an adult child who live together and care for one another receives no comparable legal recognition. The commitment between lifelong platonic friends who share finances and make end-of-life decisions for one another goes unprotected.

This discrimination is not incidental—it is structural. It flows directly from the state's decision to recognize one type of relationship above all others. The only way to eliminate this discrimination is to eliminate the privileged category itself.

V. The Social Case: Freeing Relationships from Government Surveillance

State-recognized marriage is not merely a bundle of benefits—it is also a system of surveillance and regulation. To marry, individuals must obtain a license from the state. To divorce, they must petition a court. The state monitors who is married to whom, adjudicates disputes over marital property and child custody, and imposes obligations on married individuals that do not apply to the unmarried.

This regulatory apparatus has historically been used to enforce conformity and punish deviation. Adultery has been criminalized. "Alienation of affections" lawsuits have allowed juries to punish third parties for interfering in a marriage. Cohabitation laws have criminalized unmarried couples living together. Marital rape exemptions persisted in some jurisdictions well into the late twentieth century.

While many of these abuses have been reformed, the underlying dynamic remains: the state treats marriage as a matter of public concern, entitled to public regulation. Abolishing state-recognized marriage would remove the government's jurisdiction over intimate life, leaving individuals free to structure their relationships as they see fit.

VI. Addressing Counterarguments

"Marriage is a fundamental social institution that the state must support."

Marriage is indeed a deeply rooted social institution. But deeply rooted institutions do not require state support to survive. Religion is a deeply rooted social institution, and yet in secular democracies, the state does not administer churches or mandate prayer. The continued vitality of religious life demonstrates that institutions can thrive without government endorsement. Marriage would be no different.

"Children need the stability that marriage provides."

The welfare of children is a legitimate state concern—but it is a concern that can be addressed directly, without reference to the parents' marital status. Child welfare laws, custody standards, child support enforcement, and educational policy can all be designed to protect children regardless of whether their parents are married, cohabiting, single, or in some other arrangement. Tying child welfare to marriage is not only unnecessary but counterproductive, as it stigmatizes children of unmarried parents and fails to protect children in dysfunctional married households.

"Abolishing marriage would create legal chaos."

Transitional challenges are real but manageable. A phased approach—first unbundling marriage into separate legal mechanisms, then gradually replacing the marriage category with a more flexible partnership system—could minimize disruption. Legal systems regularly undergo significant reform; the abolition of coverture, the introduction of no-fault divorce, and the legalization of same-sex marriage all required substantial legal restructuring and were accomplished without systemic collapse.

"People want to get married; the state is just facilitating their wishes."

People who want to make a public commitment to one another can still do so—through religious ceremonies, cultural rituals, personal vows, or private contracts. What they would no longer be able to do is use the state to confer legal advantages on their relationship that are denied to others. The freedom to marry, in other words, would become the freedom to celebrate one's relationship in whatever way one chooses—without the coercive apparatus of the state.

"Without state-recognized marriage, abusive partners would lose protections."

This concern is valid but misplaced. Domestic violence protections, restraining orders, and criminal law against assault and harassment do not depend on marital status and should continue to apply to all individuals regardless of their relationship configuration. In fact, some scholars have argued that the marriage framework has historically trapped abuse victims by tying their economic survival and legal status to their abuser. A reformed system that provides individual legal protections—independent of relationship status—would better serve victims of abuse.

VII. The Vision: A Society of Free Relationships

Imagine a society in which:

  • Two elderly siblings who share a home and care for each other can register a partnership that grants them the same legal protections as any romantic couple.
  • Three partners in a polyamorous family can formalize their shared obligations and rights without being told their relationship is legally invalid.
  • A single mother receives the same tax treatment, the same social recognition, and the same access to support services as a married parent.
  • Two close friends who have built a life together can designate each other as healthcare proxies and inherit from one another without a marriage license.
  • A religious community defines marriage according to its own beliefs, without any government redefinition or interference.
  • No one is pressured to marry for economic reasons, immigration status, or legal protections—because those protections are available to all, through clear and accessible legal mechanisms.

This is not a utopian fantasy. It is a practical and achievable reform that would make the legal system more equitable, more flexible, and more respectful of individual autonomy.

Conclusion

The state's involvement in marriage is a historical accident, not a moral necessity. It was born of the state's desire to regulate reproduction, control property, and enforce social conformity. It persists today as a bundle of legal privileges that discriminate against the unmarried, a regulatory apparatus that intrudes on private life, and a definitional framework that inevitably excludes those who do not conform to the majority's conception of intimate relationships.

None of this is necessary. The legal rights and protections currently tied to marriage can be made available through more flexible, equitable, and voluntary mechanisms. Religious and cultural conceptions of marriage can continue to thrive without state endorsement. And individuals can be freed to define their own relationships on their own terms.

The abolition of state-recognized marriage is not an attack on love, commitment, or family. It is a defense of these things—a recognition that they are too important, too personal, and too diverse to be reduced to a government checkbox.

It is time for the state to get out of the marriage business—and to let people love, commit, and build families on their own terms.
