Introduction

Marriage is a deeply personal institution, rooted in tradition, love, and commitment. The Problems with State-Sanctioned Marriage

1. Government Overreach into Personal Relationships

The state’s involvement in marriage represents an unjustified intrusion into private life. Why should the government have the authority to dictate who can marry, under what conditions, and with what legal consequences? Marriage is an intimate bond between individuals, and its validity should not depend on government approval. When the state regulates marriage, it imposes its own moral and legal framework on private relationships, stripping individuals of autonomy.

Consider, for example, the historical restrictions on interracial marriage, same-sex marriage, and even polyamorous relationships. The state has repeatedly used marriage law to enforce social norms, often oppressively. 2. Arbitrary and Discriminatory Application of Benefits

One of the most contentious aspects of state-recognized marriage is its role in distributing legal benefits. From tax advantages to inheritance rights, marriage confers a long list of privileges—and these privileges are not available to those who choose not to marry or cannot marry (e.g., unmarried partners, polyamorous groups, or families structured differently).

This creates an unfair system where the state arbitrarily rewards some relationships while excluding others. The lack of neutrality in marriage law creates second-class citizens based on relationship structure—a problem that would vanish if the state recognized all relationships equally (or none at all).

3. Legal Complexity and Inefficiency

The legal infrastructure surrounding marriage is cumbersome and often counterproductive. Divorce proceedings, property disputes, and child custody battles frequently become mired in bureaucratic red tape precisely because marriage is a legal institution. Couples must navigate layers of family law, and courts are forced to mediate disputes that should ideally be settled privately.

3. Eliminating Discrimination by Default

If marriage were abolished as a legal category, discrimination based on marital status would disappear. No longer would unmarried partners, polyamorous families, or cohabiting siblings be excluded from protections simply because they are not in a state-sanctioned marriage.

Conclusion: A Call for Freedom and Equality

Government regulation of marriage is an outdated and oppressive relic of a time when the state sought to control personal lives. Eliminating state recognition of marriage would end discrimination, reduce bureaucracy, and restore autonomy to individuals.

The Case for Removing Marriage from the State

Introduction

Marriage occupies a peculiar place in modern society: it is simultaneously one of the most intimate human relationships and one of the most heavily regulated. The state issues licenses, defines who may marry whom, attaches hundreds of legal consequences to marital status, and adjudicates its dissolution. This essay argues that this entanglement is neither necessary nor just, and that the state should withdraw entirely from the recognition and regulation of marriage, leaving it to be governed by private contract and personal conscience.

The Problem of State Definition

When the state defines marriage, it inevitably privileges certain relationships over others. History demonstrates this vividly. Anti-miscegenation laws barred interracial couples until 1967. Same-sex couples were excluded from legal marriage until 2015. In each case, the state's monopoly on defining marriage became a tool of exclusion, requiring decades of struggle to correct.

The deeper lesson is structural: any time the government holds the power to define a relationship, it holds the power to deny that definition to disfavored groups. Removing the state from marriage altogether eliminates this danger at its root. No future majority could weaponize marriage law against a minority if marriage law simply did not exist.

Equality and the Limits of a Single Model

Current marriage law assumes a particular relational form—typically two people in a romantic, often sexual, partnership. Yet human beings organize their lives in countless ways. Elderly siblings sharing a home, lifelong platonic friends raising children together, or larger interdependent households receive none of the legal recognition granted to married couples, despite bearing similar mutual obligations.

By bundling hundreds of legal benefits—tax treatment, inheritance defaults, hospital visitation, immigration sponsorship—into a single status, the state forces diverse relationships into one mold. A privatized, contractual approach would allow individuals to assemble precisely the legal arrangements that fit their actual lives, rather than accepting a standardized package designed for an idealized couple.

Separating Function from Status

Critics will object that marriage delivers essential legal functions. This is true, but it conflates the functions with the status. Each function can be achieved independently:

  • Property and inheritance can be arranged through wills, trusts, and joint ownership.
  • Medical decision-making can be assigned through powers of attorney and advance directives.
  • Child custody and support can—and should—be governed by laws centered on the welfare of children, which apply regardless of parents' marital status.
  • Financial interdependence can be structured through private contracts tailored to each relationship.

These tools already exist. A world without legal marriage would not be a world without legal protections; it would be a world where protections attach to chosen commitments and concrete circumstances rather than to a one-size-fits-all label.

Respecting Liberty and Conscience

Marriage carries profound religious, cultural, and personal meaning that varies enormously across communities. When the state defines marriage, it inevitably imposes one conception over others, generating perpetual conflict—witness the bitter disputes over whether civil marriage should mirror religious doctrine.

Privatizing marriage dissolves this conflict elegantly. Religious institutions could solemnize marriages according to their own teachings; secular individuals could craft their own ceremonies and contracts; communities could define marriage as they see fit. The state would neither endorse nor forbid any conception, treating all as equally valid in the eyes of the law because none would be the law's concern. This is the truest form of pluralism: not the state picking winners, but the state stepping aside.

Reducing State Intrusion

Marriage regulation invites the government into the bedroom and the household. The state currently decides what counts as a "real" marriage for immigration, scrutinizes relationships for fraud, and superintends divorce proceedings that can be invasive and adversarial. A contractual framework would treat relationship breakdowns like other contractual matters—governed by terms the parties agreed to in advance—reducing the moralistic and intrusive character of family courts.

Addressing Objections

"This would harm vulnerable spouses." On the contrary, default protections for dependents and children can be preserved through general law without requiring marriage. Indeed, many vulnerable people today—unmarried partners, cohabitants—already fall outside marriage's protections. A contract-based system, with mandatory baseline safeguards for dependents, could extend protection more broadly than the current binary of married versus unmarried.

"Marriage promotes social stability." Stable, committed relationships do benefit society—but commitment flows from the parties themselves, not from a license. People will continue to form lasting bonds and raise families. What changes is only that the state stops policing the label.

"It would create chaos and inconsistency." Contract law already manages enormous complexity across business and personal life. Standardized template agreements could provide simplicity for those who want it, while permitting customization for those who need it.

Conclusion

The state's involvement in marriage is a historical inheritance, not a logical necessity. It has repeatedly served exclusion, forced diverse human relationships into a single rigid form, and entangled government in matters of conscience that it cannot fairly adjudicate. Every legitimate function the state now performs through marriage can be accomplished through private contract and targeted laws protecting children and dependents.

To remove marriage from the legal sphere is not to devalue it—it is to liberate it, returning marriage to the individuals, families, and communities to whom it truly belongs. A free society should trust its citizens to define their own commitments. The state's proper role is to enforce the agreements people make and protect the vulnerable, not to issue licenses for love.

Why should a bureaucratic form, a fee, or a judge’s approval determine whether a couple’s commitment is valid? If two people wish to make solemn vows to each other in a religious ceremony, why must they first navigate a legal maze to gain the state’s approval?

A. The Myth of State Beneficence in Marriage

Proponents of state-regulated marriage often argue that legal recognition provides stability, financial protections, and inheritance rights. However, these benefits are not inherent to marriage itself but are economic and legal privileges granted by the state. If the government insists on providing these benefits, it should do so through neutral, contract-based means—such as inheritance law reforms, cohabitation agreements, and private insurance—not by tying them to a state-approved marriage license.

Moreover, the state’s involvement in marriage often creates perverse incentives. Governments have long used marriage laws to enforce discriminatory policies—from racial segregation under anti-miscegenation laws to restrictions on same-sex marriages. By removing marriage as a legal institution, the state would no longer have to decide which relationships are "worthy" of recognition, eliminating arbitrary discrimination.

Critics argue that without marriage as a cultural norm, society will collapse into chaos. But:

The Case for the Complete Abolition of State Marriage: Why Love Should Not Be a Legal Institution

Introduction

Marriage, as a legal institution, has long been a cornerstone of state governance, shaping social norms, economic policies, and personal freedoms. Yet, despite its historical and cultural significance, the state’s involvement in marriage is an outdated and oppressive imposition on individual autonomy. The regulation of marriage by governments—whether through licensing, taxation, or enforcement—serves no legitimate public interest but instead restricts personal freedom, reinforces outdated gender roles, and creates unnecessary bureaucratic burdens. The time has come to abolish state recognition of marriage entirely, allowing it to exist solely as a private agreement between consenting adults, free from government interference.

This essay argues that marriage should be removed from the legal sphere for five key reasons: 1) it violates individual autonomy by imposing state-mandated relationships, 2) it perpetuates harmful gender and social hierarchies, 3) it creates unnecessary legal and financial burdens, 4) it fails to serve any legitimate public interest, and 5) it undermines the principle of secular governance. By dismantling state marriage, society can foster greater personal freedom, reduce state overreach, and allow relationships to flourish without coercion.

1. Marriage as a Violation of Individual Autonomy

The most fundamental argument against state marriage is that it infringes upon personal liberty by forcing individuals into a legal framework they may not choose. Marriage is not a natural or universal human institution—it is a social construct that has evolved over centuries, often to serve patriarchal, economic, or religious purposes. Yet today, governments compel citizens to conform to this construct by granting it legal privileges, such as tax benefits, inheritance rights, and immigration advantages—all of which are coercive incentives that pressure people into marriage.

The Problem of Coercion Through Privileges

When the state grants special legal status to married couples, it effectively punishes those who choose not to marry by denying them the same benefits. For example:

  • Tax penalties for unmarried couples (e.g., the "marriage penalty" in some tax systems).
  • Denial of spousal visas for long-term partners who are not legally married.
  • Inheritance and medical decision-making rights that favor married couples over domestic partners.

These policies do not reflect a neutral public interest but rather encourage conformity to an outdated institution. If the state truly valued individual freedom, it would remove all legal distinctions between married and unmarried couples, allowing people to form relationships without government approval.

The Hypocrisy of "Civil Marriage"

Proponents of state marriage often argue that "civil marriage" (secular, non-religious marriage) is necessary to protect individuals. However, this is a false dichotomy—if the state is going to regulate relationships, it should do so equally for all, not just those who meet arbitrary legal criteria. The reality is that state marriage is inherently discriminatory because it:

  • Excludes polyamorous relationships (which are legally unrecognized in most jurisdictions).
  • Denies same-sex couples equal rights (until recently, in many places).
  • Requires bureaucratic approval, which is unnecessary for private agreements.

If the state insists on regulating relationships, it should apply the same rules to all, not just those who fit within a narrow, historically contingent definition.

The Libertarian Argument: Consenting Adults Should Define Their Own Relationships

From a libertarian perspective, the state has no legitimate authority to dictate how adults form personal bonds. Marriage, when stripped of its legal privileges, becomes nothing more than a private contract—one that can be entered into, modified, or dissolved without government interference. If two people wish to call themselves "married," they should be free to do so without a license, a ceremony, or a judge’s approval.

The only legitimate role of the state in relationships is protecting individuals from coercion and fraud—not mandating how they define their partnerships. If a couple wants to sign a private contract outlining property division, inheritance, or medical decisions, they should be able to do so without government oversight. But the state should not impose its own definition of marriage on them.

2. Marriage Perpetuates Harmful Gender and Social Hierarchies

One of the most insidious aspects of state marriage is its historical and ongoing reinforcement of patriarchal structures. While marriage has evolved in some ways, its legal framework still carries residual biases that disadvantage women, LGBTQ+ individuals, and non-traditional families.

The Legal Reinforcement of Gender Roles

Even in modern societies, marriage law often assumes a traditional family structure—one where two people (usually a man and a woman) are in a monogamous, lifelong partnership. This assumption is problematic because:

  • Divorce laws still favor one spouse over another in many cases (e.g., alimony, child custody).
  • Same-sex couples face unequal treatment in adoption, surrogacy, and parental rights.
  • Polyamorous and open relationships are legally unrecognized, forcing people into monogamy by default.

By tying legal privileges to a specific relationship structure, the state implicitly endorses certain lifestyles while marginalizing others. If marriage were purely private, individuals could define their relationships without legal coercion—whether monogamous, polyamorous, or otherwise.

The Problem of State-Enforced Monogamy

Many legal systems only recognize monogamous marriages, effectively criminalizing or penalizing polyamorous relationships. This is arbitrary and unjust—why should the state dictate how many partners an adult can have? If two people want to enter into a private, consensual, non-monogamous agreement, they should be free to do so without fear of legal repercussions.

The state has no business policing personal relationships—it should only intervene when harm is done (e.g., coercion, abuse). But by favoring monogamy in law, the state imposes its moral preferences on citizens.

Marriage as a Tool of Social Control

Historically, marriage has been used to control women’s sexuality, labor, and property rights. Even today, many legal systems treat married women differently in matters of inheritance, employment, and citizenship. For example:

  • Spousal rape was not criminalized in all U.S. states until the 1990s because marriage was seen as a "license" for sexual access.
  • Many countries still have laws that disadvantage unmarried mothers in child custody battles.
  • Immigration policies often favor married couples over unmarried partners, forcing people into marriage for legal benefits.

If marriage were purely private, these structural inequalities would not exist—people would be free to form relationships without legal coercion.

3. The Bureaucratic and Financial Burdens of State Marriage

Beyond its moral and social problems, state marriage is inefficient, costly, and unnecessary. The bureaucratic overhead of licensing, enforcing, and dissolving marriages wastes public resources that could be better spent elsewhere.

The Cost of Marriage Licensing and Enforcement

Every year, governments spend millions (or billions) of dollars on:

  • Issuing marriage licenses (which require paperwork, fees, and administrative work).
  • Enforcing marriage laws (e.g., divorce proceedings, child support, property disputes).
  • Processing marriage-based benefits (tax filings, social security, immigration).

These costs could be eliminated if marriage were purely private. Instead of requiring a government-issued license, couples could simply sign a private contract (or none at all) to define their relationship terms.

The Financial Incentives That Distort Relationships

The state’s tax breaks, inheritance privileges, and social security benefits for married couples create perverse incentives that encourage people to marry for legal advantages rather than personal commitment. For example:

  • Tax deductions for married couples (which can be larger than for unmarried couples in some cases).
  • Survivor benefits (e.g., Social Security spousal benefits).
  • Estate tax exemptions for married couples.

These policies do not reflect genuine social value but rather subsidize marriage as an economic institution. If the state removed these incentives, people would be free to choose relationships based on love, not legal privileges.

The Problem of Divorce: A State-Created Mess

Divorce is one of the most contentious and expensive legal processes in many countries. Because marriage is a state-sanctioned contract, dissolving it requires court intervention, property division, alimony negotiations, and child custody battles—all of which are costly, stressful, and often unfair.

If marriage were purely private, couples could agree on their own terms for separation (e.g., through a private mediation contract) without involving the state. This would reduce conflict, lower costs, and give individuals more control over their lives.

4. The State Has No Legitimate Interest in Regulating Marriage

Opponents of marriage abolition often argue that the state must regulate marriage to protect individuals. However, this claim does not hold up under scrutiny—the state already has alternative mechanisms to protect people without imposing marriage.

The Myth of "Protecting Vulnerable Parties"

Some argue that marriage laws protect spouses from fraud or abuse. But this is false—the state already has stronger legal tools to address these issues:

  • Contracts law allows couples to privately define their rights and obligations without government interference.
  • Family law already handles domestic violence, child custody, and property disputes—regardless of marital status.
  • Criminal law protects individuals from coercion and abuse—marriage status does not change this.

If a person is tricked into a relationship, they can sue for fraud under contract law. If a spouse abuses their partner, they can file for restraining orders or criminal charges. The state does not need marriage to protect people—it already has better tools to do so.

The Slippery Slope of State-Approved Relationships

If the state approves some relationships (marriage) but not others (polyamory, cohabitation), it is picking winners and losers. This is arbitrary and unjust. Why should the state favor monogamous, heterosexual couples over other forms of partnership?

A consistent libertarian position would be to remove all legal distinctions between relationships. If the state must regulate personal bonds (which it shouldn’t), it should do so equally—not pick and choose which ones get privileges.

The Historical Precedent: Marriage Was Never Universal

Marriage, as a legal institution, is a recent invention—most of human history has not recognized it in the way modern states do. Many cultures have alternative relationship structures, such as:

  • Polygamy (historically common in many societies).
  • Group marriages (e.g., the Mosuo people of China).
  • Cohabitation without legal ties (common in many European countries).

If marriage were purely private, societies could adapt to different relationship models without state interference.

5. Marriage Undermines Secular Governance

One of the most ironic and hypocritical aspects of state marriage is that it blurs the line between church and state. While many argue that "civil marriage" is secular, the legal privileges attached to marriage are inherently religious in origin—they were designed to enforce Christian (or other religious) values on society.

The Religious Origins of Marriage Law

Marriage laws in Western countries were originally Christian doctrines that:

  • Banned divorce (until the 20th century).
  • Restricted marriage to heterosexual couples.
  • Required religious ceremonies (in many places, until recently).

Even today, many countries allow religious officials to perform marriages, meaning the state is delegating its authority to religious institutions—a clear violation of secularism.

The Problem of State-Enforced Morality

When the state grants special legal status to marriage, it is endorsing a particular moral view—that monogamous, heterosexual relationships are superior. This is discriminatory because:

  • It excludes LGBTQ+ couples (until recently).
  • It penalizes polyamorous relationships.
  • It favors traditional family structures over others.

A truly secular state should not be in the business of promoting or restricting personal relationships. If the state must regulate anything, it should do so neutrally—not impose its own moral preferences.

The Alternative: Private Contracts and Secular Relationships

Instead of state-approved marriage, individuals could:

  • Sign private contracts outlining their rights and obligations.
  • Use secular ceremonies (e.g., civil partnerships, cohabitation agreements).
  • Define their relationships without government interference.

This would remove the religious and moral baggage from marriage while still allowing people to form meaningful bonds.

Counterarguments and Rebuttals

Counterargument: "But what about children’s rights?"

Some argue that marriage is necessary to protect children’s welfare. However, this is already handled by family law—children’s rights are not tied to marriage status. Unmarried parents have the same legal obligations as married ones. If anything, state marriage can be harmful because it encourages people to stay in abusive relationships for the sake of their children.

This is already solvable—couples could sign private contracts that are legally binding without requiring a marriage license. Tax and inheritance laws could be reformed to treat all couples equally, regardless of marital status.

Social stability is not the state’s job—it is the result of voluntary cooperation. If people choose to marry (or not), they will form stable relationships without government coercion. Conclusion: The Time Has Come to Abolish State Marriage

Marriage, as a legal institution, is outdated, oppressive, and unnecessary. It violates individual autonomy, perpetuates harmful hierarchies, creates bureaucratic burdens, and serves no legitimate public interest. The state has no business regulating personal relationships—it should remove all legal distinctions between married and unmarried couples and allow people to define their bonds freely.

By abolishing state marriage, society would: ✅ Restore individual freedom—people would no longer be forced into legal frameworks they don’t choose. ✅ Eliminate discriminatory policies—polyamorous, LGBTQ+, and non-traditional relationships would no longer be marginalized. ✅ Reduce government overreach—millions of dollars could be saved by eliminating marriage licensing and enforcement. ✅ Promote secular governance—the state would no longer be in the business of imposing religious or moral preferences on citizens. ✅ Allow relationships to flourish naturally—love and commitment would no longer be coerced by legal privileges.

The abolition of state marriage is not an attack on love—it is a defense of liberty. If two people wish to call themselves "married," they should be free to do so without government approval. If they wish to sign a private contract outlining their rights, they should be free to do that as well. But the state should not have the power to dictate, regulate, or punish personal relationships.

It is time to dismantle state marriage and return relationships to the private sphere, where they belong. Only then can society truly embrace freedom, equality, and personal autonomy.
